technical instance is essentially an expansion of its tree, starting from the root—the technical element itself—and adding nodes that are related to it, complement it, form part of it, support it, operate it, etc. see the worked case in qa below (### (case study) what is the recursively decomposed instance tree of a crm system?). read the case table as the worked in-path-typed tree: the empty table here is filled the same way, typing each row from its grouping segments and the declared root binding. technical element type tree path: the expansion path typing one instance row (fourth column) — (root) := <<technical element bound to the row's table type, continued by exactly one licensed expansion: a spine-ordered suffix or a composite nesting. in other words, a tree path is what the single table generates. it is a type-level path ( - ), never to be confused with the instance tree path (first column), which strings instances with → . constructing the path: (1) type the instance — find its row in the table above; (2) bind — write (root) := <<technical element as that type; (3) extend — continue with exactly one licensed expansion from the bound position (spine-ordered suffix or composite nesting under the bound root); (4) check — single types and spine-ordered chains always license; anything else must match a nested composite. the tree is governed by the following rules: root: the root is the technical element type to which the technical instance being decomposed belongs or is related. structure: intermediate nodes provide the structure needed to organize the decomposition - they can be technical instances - or technical types. technical types cannot be the final nodes in the tree - may be used as grouping nodes, but they are not themselves instances. leaves: every leaf must resolve to a technical instance. typing: every instance is typed — by its fourth-column tree path where the table carries one, otherwise by its nearest enclosing grouping segment, with the decomposition root's type declared once. recursion: any technical instance identified in the tree may itself be decomposed recursively. well-formedness: an instance decomposition is well-formed when every instance row's type path is a path the table generates: bind (root) := <<technical element to the root instance's type and continue down-branch in order; branch order is never skipped. any row may serve as a decomposition root for recursive decomposition. no repetition: the root's own type must not be unnecessarily repeated as an intermediate grouping node. exception: a same-type segment is allowed when it scopes a genuine instance family that would otherwise hang untyped (e.g. a technical standard grouping scoping the standards family inside a biotechnology decomposition, whose fourth-column counterpart is (root) := <<technical element - ... - technical standard ); a same-type segment with only generic description and no scoping function stays forbidden. well-form instance tree path rule: ensure the decomposition provides a rich set of intermediate (internals) nodes - both - type and instances, aiding understanding. the set of intermediate instance nodes representing relationships such as subtyping, composition, support, dependency, or other useful structural relationships. style rules for intermediate nodes instances: style intermediate nodes that represent actual technical instances as plain text (no adornment). naming: name every instance node in title case — capitalize every whitespace- or hyphen-separated word ( contact record - contact record , stage-entry criterion - stage-entry criterion ); preserve established all-caps acronyms ( api , crm ). type segments keep their table casing. the rule governs node names in instance tree paths only; descriptions stay sentence-case prose. composite instance naming : a composite instance — a nested ensemble (a technical element set , production technical system , technical practice , or sub-domain set), not an ordinary object, record, or mechanism — takes a name ending in set once it sits at a depth greater than 2. depth counts every segment of the instance tree path, backticked type groupings included, the root type grouping being depth 1. at depth 2 or less the suffix is permitted but never required: technical element set - pharmaceutical technical domain set (depth 2) keeps it, technical element set - drug discovery set (depth 3) requires it. types: style bare technical element types used as grouping nodes as code . distinction: never style an instance and a type in the same way; the distinction must be immediately visible. grouping types: a type used only to group instances is not itself an instance and must not terminate a branch. the path link - is →. technical element type tree path : in the definition table this column is a template carrying the <<technical element root slot; once the root instance's type is bound ( (root) := … ), the instantiated path contains only concrete technical element types — no expansion patterns or placeholders. instance tree path description technical category technical element type tree path --- --- --- --- terminology the terms used across this note — technique, artifact, system, object, mechanism, process, function, capability, verification, validation, and the technical family — are defined in the glossarium. qa what type of technical element is a conveyor belt? a conveyor belt is equipment, not a producer — unless relocation is itself the delivered good. the test: does the element transform reality itself into the good that is delivered? - producer when the transformation is the service being delivered: a parcel depot's sorting conveyor delivers delivered goods — matter relocated to its destination is the good — so it types as a service good producer (or material good producer when the delivered good is the relocated material itself). - support when it only carries another producer's output to the next station: the same belt inside a bottling line transforms nothing and produces nothing; it is a production equipment implement attached under the bound producing technical element , never a producer itself. the same rule demotes the other supports: a production facility houses production, a production instrument meters it, a production tool bears on the workpiece, a machine names the drive package — none transforms reality on its own. capacity alone is not production; transformation of reality is. what type of technical element is a llm? an llm is a virtual informational technical object : an engineered computational artifact whose structure is constituted primarily by software, learned parameters, representations, and computational procedures rather than by directly observable physical structure. its technical functions are realized through computation executed on physical infrastructure. on the bad use of the term ‘technology’? technology — properly, the systematic study, knowledge, or theory of technique and technical elements ; in everyday language, however, technology is commonly used metonymically to refer to the technical elements themselves —especially technical objects, systems, and artifacts. what is the most abstract formulation that operation can take? - requirements → technique → product (good, service). - desired difference → controlled transformation → realized difference. what is the relationship between technical function and technical capability ? note: technical capability and technical function are closely related and overlapping. function is the raw concept: what the artifact does . capability refers to the value or possibility enabled by that function : what the function makes possible . is every function realized through a mechanism? yes. a function is realized by a mechanism that produces the required effect. however, mechanism is a more abstract concept than process : the same mechanism can realize different functions, depending on how it is organized or operated. is a mechanism identical to an underlying process? no. a mechanism is not necessarily identical to a single underlying process. a mechanism may coordinate or combine multiple processes to realize a function. conversely, the same underlying process may participate in different mechanisms and contribute to different functions. what is the relation between function, mechanism and process? function = what is achieved. mechanism = how the function is realized. process = an organized sequence of transformations or events that may constitute part of the mechanism. what is the relation between 'technical capability' and 'technical function'? a technical capability is a latent functionality: a function that a technical element is capable of exercising but is not currently exercising. a technical function is a capability being exercised in operation. a technical decomposition describes the structure of a technical element, not its real-time operation; therefore, specifying its technical function is not necessary . what is the relation between technical practice and technical activity ? technical practice is the pattern; technical activity is the pattern exercised in time. a practice organizes what recurs — activities, techniques, principles, standards, tools; an activity is one scheduled exercising of it — brief → build → launch → monitor → close. every activity belongs to a practice the way every exercised function belongs to a capability: the same duality, temporal instead of modal. do we actually need technical activity as a technical element in the decomposition of a technical element, or is it already covered by technical practice , similar to the relationship between technical function and technical capability ? no. a fully specified technical practice —including its tasks, techniques, acts, standards, and control gates—leaves no additional structural role for technical activity to contribute. an activity is the temporal instantiation of a practice : it describes the practice as it is actually being performed over time. like technical function , it therefore describes operation rather than structure and is not necessary for the structural decomposition of a technical element. why is the category technical element set required? a technical element set is required to represent coherent technical ensembles whose members belong to different technical element types but are related through a common technical object, standard, capability, production process, or technical domain. without this category, the taxonomy can describe the individual elements of such an ensemble, but it lacks a type for representing the ensemble itself as a technical entity of organization . take as example: the openapi technical ecosystem. it comprises the openapi specification (oas), openapi documents, annotations, generators, plugins, libraries, validation tools, documentation tools, and generated artifacts. these elements have different technical element types, but are related through the common purpose of specifying, producing, validating, documenting, and consuming api interfaces. the technical element set category provides a type for representing this coherent ensemble as a whole. why shouldn't technical knowledge be a technical element type? technical knowledge should not be a technical-element type because knowledge is already represented by the taxonomy as a distinct ontological category; making it a technical element would conflate the knowledge about a technical reality with the technical reality itself. why do we need a technical domain reality model type ? a technical domain reality model fills the ontological gap between reality itself and the technical practice that operates upon it . it represents the bounded, operative model of the relevant domain reality —its entities, structures, processes, states, resources, interfaces, paths, and constraints—needed to make technical operations intelligible and executable. a technical domain reality model is needed because technical activity requires a bounded model of the part of reality it acts upon. it provides the domain-specific reality structure against which technical elements are defined, coordinated, executed, constrained, and evaluated. notes.text: philosophia conceptuum et operis in this note, we will explore the abstract concept of a concept 😄. a concept can be understood as a cognitive tool used to parse, categorize, and make sense of reality . formulation what is the concept of a concept? why is a function, a country, red, etc concepts? a structured, constraint-imposing representational operator that partitions a domain of possible states into equivalence classes under a set of invariances, enabling compression, inference, and action. a concept induces a discretization over the flux of events in reality and its ontic substrate - enabling inteligibilty. a concept types (tags)(categorized) of flux of realty - into a discrete stream - it takes several pieces of the flux - and map it to one tag. - it’s not only abou y as gilles deleuze and félix guattari rigorously argued, a concept is not a given; it is a constructed entity. it is a topological "cut" made in the continuum of the real. a concept does not passively reflect reality; it actively intervenes in it. it draws boundaries where nature knows none. to conceptualize "forest" or "justice" is to extract a set of properties from the infinite fabric of the universe and hold them together in a specific, intentional configuration. the concept is the scaffold, not the building. at its most rigorous, a concept is fundamentally an epistemic tool engineered to perform a discrete cut upon a continuous, undivided ontic substrate . it is not merely a psychological artifact, a linguistic placeholder, or a static representation; rather, it is an active, structural boundary that isolates and delineates a specific segment of reality . concepts are the units by which cognition factorizes reality; the concept of a concept is the theory of those factorization operators. ontology what is the ontological nature of the entity ‘concept’? in which level of the representation hierarchy does concept belong? the entity ‘concept’ is an abstract, intentional entity that exists in thought or representation, lacking physical substance but capable of being instantiated in cognition, language, or symbolic systems. aspect description note --- --- --- substantiality does the entity have a material or substantial basis? concepts are non-substantial ; they exist mentally or intentionally, not physically. instantiability can the entity exist in concrete instances or is it abstract? abstract, but can be instantiated in thought, symbolic representations, language, or diagrams. temporal persistence how long does the entity exist over time? persists as long as it is recognized, remembered, recorded, or communicated ; potentially indefinite. cognitive accessibility can the entity be perceived, thought about, or known? directly accessible to cognition; can be reasoned about, analyzed, and communicated . conventional dependency does the entity exist due to social or linguistic conventions? partially dependent; specific names, frameworks, or symbolic representations rely on human conventions, but the underlying concept can exist independently in thought. dependence does the entity require other entities to exist? dependent on cognitive agents or symbolic systems ; cannot exist independently in the physical world. causality can the entity produce effects or be affected? influences thinking, decision-making, social structures, and communication ; its effects are mediated through human action. level of existence in which level of the representation hierarchy does concept belong? second-order existence - althout is tricky - becasd the concept of a ‘type’ at which level it’s - ‘concept’ is lower level than ‘the concept of a type’ == ‘type’ theory note: conceptions of concepts usually come from a larger theory of cognition. theory description evaluation key proponents --- --- --- --- classical theory concepts defined by necessary and sufficient conditions (e.g., "bachelor" = unmarried male). strengths: logical precision, compositionality, supports formal reasoning. failures: empirically invalid for most natural categories (no strict boundaries). scope: works for formal, legal, and mathematical concepts. aristotle, john locke prototype theory concepts organized around a central prototype , with graded membership. strengths: matches human categorization behavior (typicality effects). failures: lacks compositionality; weak for abstract/relational concepts. scope: perceptual and everyday categories. eleanor rosch, george lakoff exemplar theory concepts are sets of stored instances ; categorization via similarity to exemplars. strengths: high empirical fidelity; captures variability. failures: memory-intensive; poor abstraction/generalization. scope: small-scale, experience-driven domains. edward e. smith, douglas medin theory-theory concepts embedded in naive causal-explanatory theories . strengths: explains conceptual change, depth, and causality. failures: underspecified structure; difficult to formalize computationally. scope: scientific reasoning, child development, abstract domains. alison gopnik, frank keil neoclassical theory concepts defined by weighted feature structures rather than strict rules. strengths: bridges classical and probabilistic views. failures: feature selection is ad hoc; lacks deep structure. scope: intermediate-level categorization tasks. amos tversky, daniel kahneman dynamic frame theory concepts are context-activated frames with structured roles. strengths: captures context sensitivity and relational structure. failures: hard to formalize rigorously; frame boundaries unclear. scope: language, semantics, narrative cognition. charles j. fillmore, george lakoff embodied cognition concepts grounded in sensorimotor systems and bodily interaction. strengths: neurobiological plausibility; explains grounding. failures: weak on abstraction (math, logic). scope: action-related and perceptual concepts. george lakoff, mark johnson, vittorio gallese conceptual atomism concepts are primitive, indivisible symbols with fixed reference. strengths: avoids circular definitions; supports compositional semantics. failures: no learning account; ignores structure. scope: theoretical semantics, philosophy of mind. jerry fodor pragmatic / contextualist concepts are use-dependent tools , meaning emerges in context. strengths: captures flexibility and real-world usage. failures: risks relativism; weak predictive power. scope: language use, social cognition. ludwig wittgenstein, saul kripke probabilistic view concepts represented as probability distributions over features or hypotheses. strengths: normative (bayesian), handles uncertainty and generalization. failures: computationally expensive; depends on priors. scope: machine learning, cognitive modeling. joshua tenenbaum, tom griffiths dynamic systems theory of cognition concepts emerge from nonlinear dynamical interactions in cognitive systems. strengths: captures temporal evolution and emergence. failures: low interpretability; difficult symbolic mapping. scope: development, real-time cognition. esther thelen, linda b. smith predictive processing concepts are hierarchical generative models minimizing prediction error. strengths: unifies perception, action, and learning; strong formalism. failures: often too general (theory of everything risk). scope: neuroscience, ai, perception-action loops. karl friston, andy clark concept space type description --- --- descriptive aim to describe or categorize reality as it is (e.g., “tree,” “market,” “state”). analytical used to analyze structures or relations within reality (e.g., “power,” “capital,” “system”). normative carry value judgments or prescribe ideals and standards (e.g., “justice,” “freedom,” “chrematistics” as critique). scientific concept a term or construct embedded in a theory , operationalized and measurable, used to generate testable predictions (e.g., mass, gene, neuron). effective abstraction a higher-level model or metaphor that summarizes complex processes but may not directly map onto physical entities (e.g., “center of gravity,” “ecosystem health,” “software bug”). strategic (agentic) <<concepts used to intervene in, steer, or manipulate systems , often combining descriptive + analytical content but optimized for action rather than truth. they may be simplified, partial, or intentionally coarse. (e.g., “development model,” “market liberalization,” “industrial policy,” “containment strategy”, “overproduction”). evaluation how to evaluate concept ? criteria description (diagnostic focus) --- --- internal consistency the internal, logical integrity of the boundary rule. does the formal specification of the concept (the intentional operator) contain logical contradictions? a concept must be mathematically and philosophically sound in the abstract before it is ever applied to a given situation or context. extensional fidelity the precision of the ontological cut. how cleanly does the concept map to the underlying reality? high fidelity means the concept captures its intended target with minimal "leakage" (capturing phenomena it shouldn't) and minimal "truncation" (failing to capture phenomena it should). it measures the sharpness of the boundary. ontological parsimony the degree of structural orthogonality. does this concept carve out a genuinely novel vector in the state space, or is it heavily collinear with existing concepts? a rigorous concept must justify its existence by not multiplying variables unnecessarily. it should not overlap redundantly with established tools. epistemic leverage the functional, analytical yield. what operational work does the concept perform? once the cut is made, does it simplify a complex system, expose hidden mechanisms, or enable new computational or logical operations? a concept with low leverage is a stagnant abstraction; high leverage generates predictive or explanatory momentum. contextual robustness the invariance of the concept across varying situations. how stable is the concept when the environmental parameters or observing conditions change? a highly robust concept maintains its structural identity and explanatory power even as the underlying dynamical system shifts across different experimental or observational situations. combinatorial fluidity the capacity for systemic integration. how seamlessly can this concept be mathematically or logically coupled with other concepts within a broader epistemic scaffolding? a concept should not exist in total isolation; it must possess "hooks" that allow it to function as a node in a larger, coherent model of reality. inferential productivity capacity to support valid reasoning, predictions, or derivations (does it enable non-trivial inferences?). discriminative power ability to distinguish relevant cases from non-cases (i.e., does it carve reality at useful joints?). case study conceptual tractability: the degree to which a concept can be clearly, precisely, and consistently defined, operationalized, and applied within a theoretical or empirical framework. concept internal consistency extensional fidelity ontological parsimony epistemic leverage contextual robustness combinatorial fluidity inferential productivity discriminative power --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- nation weak–moderate (competing definitions: ethnic vs civic; benedict anderson) weak (diaspora leakage, multi-ethnic truncation) low (overlaps with culture, ethnicity, polity) moderate (mobilization, identity) weak (historically unstable meaning) moderate (interfaces ambiguously with state, culture) low (limited predictive capacity) weak (unclear boundaries) state strong (formalized; max weber) high (maps to institutions) high (distinct construct) high (governance, coercion, capacity) high (cross-context stable) high (integrates with law, economics) high (supports causal reasoning) high (clear partition: state vs non-state) country weak (ambiguous: state/territory/culture) moderate (works informally) low (redundant with state/territory) low (minimal analytical utility) moderate (stable colloquially) low (poor formal integration) very low (no real inference) weak (imprecise classification) the west very weak (no stable boundary rule) very low (massive leakage/truncation) very low (collapses many dimensions) low–moderate (narrative use only) very weak (context-dependent) low (hard to formalize) low (vague generalizations) very weak (no clean partition) civilization weak–moderate (multiple definitions) moderate (coarse-grained fit) moderate (overlaps with culture/society) moderate–high (macro-history; arnold toynbee) moderate (partially stable) moderate (usable in history frameworks) moderate (pattern-level inference) moderate (broad distinctions only) development model (term more than concept) moderate–high (can be formalized) (a platonic concept - that almost never match any realty - and if it do - it’s temporal) low ( depends on operationalization ) high (distinct analytical construct) high (comparative and causal analysis) moderate (context sensitivity) high (fits econ/political systems) high (policy and trajectory inference) moderate–high (distinguishes growth regimes) the chinese model moderate (often underspecified) moderate–high (empirically grounded in china) moderate (overlaps with development model) high (state-led development analysis) moderate (limited transferability) high (fits political economy frameworks) high (causal hypothesis generation) high (distinct from neoliberal models) kant on concepts “thoughts without content are empty; intuitions without concepts are blind.” — critique of pure reason - concepts ( begriffe ) are mental representations or thoughts that allow us to think objects . - a concept is a rule or principle for synthesizing diverse sensory intuitions into a unified representation. - concepts are general and mediate knowledge : they are universal (apply to many particular cases) and allow the mind to categorize experience. - kant distinguishes between: - empirical concepts : derived from experience (e.g., “dog,” “tree”). - pure concepts (categories) : a priori concepts that structure all possible experience (e.g., causality, substance, unity). these are necessary conditions for experience. - concepts without intuition (sensory data) are empty ; intuitions without concepts are blind . knowledge requires both. - concepts function to organize and structure sensory data, enabling cognition and objective knowledge. on definition a precise specification of the meaning of a symbol, term, or expression within a formal, linguistic, or conceptual system, typically by establishing identity, necessary and sufficient conditions, or construction rules. elements : - precise specification : a definition aims to remove ambiguity by clearly delimiting what the term denotes. - meaning of a symbol or term : this can apply to variables in formal languages, words in natural language, or constructs in mathematics and logic. - within a system : every definition is context-dependent—its validity and function are relative to a framework (e.g. set theory, a programming language, a scientific theory). - establishing identity : often in mathematics and logic, a definition takes the form of identity (e.g. a:=ba := ba:=b). - necessary and sufficient conditions : classical definitions often aim to specify all and only the instances where a term applies. - construction rules : in constructive mathematics or type theory, definitions may describe how an object is built or derived. taxonomy: 1. stipulative – introduces new terminology or assigns meaning arbitrarily within a system (e.g. "let a 'quarkon' be any particle with..."). 2. lexical – reports conventional usage (more common in natural language studies). 3. precising – narrows an existing vague term for specific analytical purposes. 4. theoretical – embeds a term within a broader theoretical framework (e.g., "force" in newtonian mechanics). 5. recursive/inductive – defines an entity by reference to itself under constraints (e.g., definition of natural numbers via peano axioms). 6. operational – defines a concept in terms of measurement or procedure (common in empirical sciences). ❓ qa what is the reptarget of a concept? can concepts represent everything other mental representations represent? representation target (reptarget): - categories (class of objects, abstract properties or tags) : grouping many instances under a common identity (“dog,” “justice”). - abstract dynamics : through compression into schemas (“orbit,” “feedback loop”). - stable structures : relatively invariant properties or relations (“triangular,” “capital city”). what concepts struggle to represent: no, concepts are not the only type of mental representation: - continuous, fine-grained detail - a concept like “red” doesn’t capture the exact shade, texture, or spectral profile. - sensory impressions (imagery, percepts) handle this better. - procedural / motor know-how - knowing the concept “ride a bike” isn’t the same as having the embodied skill. - procedural representations (muscle memory, sensorimotor schemas) are not reducible to concepts. - temporal unfolding in real time - a concept like “melody” points to structure, but to actually experience it requires a dynamic, time-based representation (auditory memory, sequence coding). - context-dependent fluidity - concepts are discrete categories; real-world phenomena are often fuzzy, continuous, overlapping. - dynamic mental models or simulations capture these better. - nonconceptual content - many philosophers argue we can have mental states (like a baby seeing red, or an animal navigating space) that are not structured conceptually but still guide action. why we need other representational formats? there are several kinds of mental representations beyond concepts, including: - concepts : compressed, communicable, categorical. - images / perceptual representations : high-resolution, modality-specific, analog. - procedures : embodied, sequential, skill-based. - schemas / mental models : structural, relational, dynamic simulations. - emotions / affective states : evaluative, motivational signals not captured by concepts. what makes a concept hard to define? … challenge description --- --- vagueness the concept has unclear or fuzzy boundaries. context-dependence meaning shifts based on cultural, disciplinary, or situational context. polysemy the concept has multiple related meanings. family resemblance no single set of features applies to all cases—only overlapping similarities. epistemic inaccessibility the concept refers to something not yet fully understood. theoretical entanglement the concept is deeply embedded in a contested or evolving theory. constructive/process-based the concept is defined through construction or procedure, not static criteria. what should we do with intractable concepts? … strategy description goal --- --- --- decompose break the concept into smaller, more manageable parts. reduce complexity by isolating components. reframe translate the concept into a different domain or metaphor. make it more intelligible through a shift in perspective. operationalize define the concept in terms of observable behavior or measurable outputs. make it testable or applicable. contextualize analyze the historical, cultural, or disciplinary background. understand the function the concept serves in its original context. sit with it accept that understanding may be slow, recursive, or experiential. let insight emerge through time or intuition. use a proxy definition create a simplified, functional stand-in that captures the concept’s practical effects. enable reasoning or communication without full clarity. abandon or circumvent recognize when a concept is unproductive or misleading and set it aside. avoid wasting resources on confusing or unproductive ideas. can we have a concept about a particular instance? in its technical sense, the term concept denotes a mental representation that captures the essential features shared by a class of instances (processes, objects, and the like). a rule, schema, or invariant that maps multiple concrete instances into a shared cognitive or inferential role. which are the limits of concept as epistemic artifact to model the world? …. references - cognitive - guia mayor - a guide to study - a guide to language and cognition - idea - notes.text: philosophia moralis et operis reality is the total set of phenomena, entities, and processes that exist or occur, independently of an observer's perception or conceptualization, and which can, in principle, interact, change, or produce effects. philosophia moralis is the scaffolding used to deliberate, and render assessable, right action — the binding claims through which agents owe, judge, and answer to one another. this note systematizes a philosophy of the moral art that can serve as a conceptual foundation for organizing the ideas used to evaluate conduct across diverse domains. it is the complement of philosophia artium technicarum et operis (which systematizes intervention), philosophia artium epistemicarum et operis (which systematizes intelligibility), and philosophia socialium et operis (which systematizes association): where those notes ask how reality is transformed, known, and coordinated, this one asks what ought to be done and who answers for it. fiduciary stewardship is a training ground for rigorous moral modeling because it enforces observable, feedback-rich answerability under conflict: a steward holds another's good in trust, acts under explicit duties, and is judged on disclosure, loyalty, and care. the value lies in transferring this answerability discipline — rather than its specific codes — into more complex domains like polities and networked collectives. index formulation what is the nature of moral practice ? moral practice: (reality; agency, claims) → right action & answerability. a moral activity is any operation performed by an agent to deliberate among binding claims, act rightly under them, judge conduct as right or wrong, and answer for what was done. the goal of the moral art is (1) to construct and maintain the scaffolding mechanisms of deliberation and judgment, and (2) to stabilize the repertoires of right action — kept promises, disclosed truths, repaired breaches — through which agents remain worthy of trust. what is the nature of the moral ? the moral is the assessability dimension of reality: the aspect under which an act can be right or wrong, permissible or impermissible, worthy of praise or blame — rendered tractable through the frame m = <a,c,j,r : the agent who acts, the claims binding the act, the judgment verdicting it, and the responsibility answering for it. what is the role of morality in human experience? morality enables agents to bind themselves across time and to one another: to make promises that hold, to hold goods in trust, to judge breaches without collapsing into vengeance, and to repair what wrongdoing breaks. every promise kept, every truth disclosed against interest, every harm owned and repaired is the recursive coupling of freedom with answerability. the labour of moral practice goes hand in hand with a layout of reality — that is its deliberative template: every moral move presupposes a parsing of who owes what to whom under which claim, and every claim earns its keep through judged use. what is a moral element ? it is a concept that denotes an element participating in the deliberation-oriented and answerability-oriented dimension of conduct experienced by humans or other purposeful agents. note: this is a deliberately loose definition of the reality denoted by the concept. foundation - reality - the ontological substrate comprising the agents, acts, consequences, goods, and binding claims that constrain and respond to moral action. person, promise, trust fund,commons, patient, mandate. what grounds moral practice ? moral practice is grounded in the lived experience of being claimed by another: the entrusting look, the reliance already placed, the harm already risked — the pre-given horizon of mutual answerability within which every choice already finds itself. agents (deliberative loci of choice), consciences (internal capacities for approval and self-accusation), and traditions (transmitted morphologies of precepts and exemplars) are crystallizations of this ground, not its foundation: they name how the claim–answer pairing stabilizes into recognizable offices and codes, never what makes the pairing possible. what is the reality we seek to act rightly within? observer-independent reality as the substrate of answerability: agents, acts, consequences, goods at stake, and the claims — duties, rights, and warranted expectations — that bind agents to one another across that substrate. reality is decomposed for deliberation in the moral order tree below. at which level of organization do we answer? the hierarchical stratification of choice and its reverberation, from punctual acts to formed character and shared orders — crucial when judging conduct with nested agency and multi-scale effects. - micro-level: individual acts and their immediate claims. - meso-level: offices, mandates, and communities of responsibility. - macro-level: traditions, orders of right, settled character of collectives. what is the ontology of the target? what is reality like as assessable? which agents, acts, claims, and judgments make it up? ontology answers by constraining what can be owed and judged; its constructs for parsing (agents, acts, goods, principles, duties, judgments, responsibilities) live in the moral order tree below, read always against imputability and tradition. how can we characterize the moral aspect of human experience? a taxonomy (conceptual structure) that renders the deliberation-oriented and answerability-oriented practice of agents intelligible. the labour of moral practice goes hand in hand with a layout of reality — that is its deliberative template: every act presupposes a parsing of who owes what to whom, and every claim earns its keep through judged use. note: moral element type is recursive. the type of order of every moral element is the moral order ; the single table below holds its branch, (root) := <<moral element (agents, acts, goods, norms, judgments, responsibilities, compounds, dynamics). each branch root carries its path and child rows extend it; child descriptions state the role-in-parent, canonical definitions live on root rows. scaffold rows are those supporting, structuring, or verdicting action — deliberations, principles, judgments, traditions, states, responsibilities, repairs; the rest are morality's agents, acts, and goods. note on imputability: every moral element is read against four conditions. capacity holds whether the agent can deliberate and do otherwise; knowledge holds what the agent could foresee; freedom holds whether coercion, deception, or necessity defeats choice; stakes holds what goods stand to be harmed or secured. the same name under defeated versus intact imputability denotes two readings, decomposed separately. note on traditions: a tradition is an analytically distinct transmitted morphology defined by its precepts, exemplars, and casuistry (fiduciary care, oath-keeping, medical stewardship, civic republicanism…), not a container of agents. traditions scope inquiry; they never own nodes. note on generic composites: different names may be used to refer to generic composites of moral elements, such as moral domain , moral order , ethical system , or similar concepts. for simplicity we use moral compound as the generic type; ensemble scopes (stewardship compacts, ward communities) bind the placeholder as moral compound . the composite community of responsibility heads compound nesting alongside it. recursion is introduced by allowing a composite to have another composite as an instance: a moral compound may contain moral compound s (a ward-care compact within a harbor stewardship compact). nesting composites in composites is what makes the type tree recursive. spines (adapted to the moral): act-spine moral agent - conscience - moral act - practice / habit ; normative-spine value / good - principle / maxim - duty / obligation - right . flat judgment types land directly under the bound root element. an instance table may land at any depth of a spine; intermediate levels are structuring types, never skipped. note on relations: regarding instance decomposition and the recursive view of the moral element type tree, the relations between elements are not specified in this document and are intentionally left open for now. each type with precept / code articulated protocol stabilizing right action within a tradition. hippocratic oath, stewardship charter, professional code deliberation (root) := <<moral element - moral dilemma / conflict situation in which binding claims collide with no costless exit. obedience versus disclosure; loyalty versus safety deliberation (root) := <<moral element - deliberation process weighing claims, consequences, and precedents toward choice. case conference, conscience examination, ethics review deliberation (root) := <<moral element - decision / choice punctual resolution of deliberation into an owned act. to disclose; to refuse; to escalate judgment (root) := <<moral element - moral judgment verdict attributing right/wrong, permissible/impermissible to conduct. acquittal, condemnation, exoneration with warning judgment (root) := <<moral element - justification / excuse warrant sustaining or defeating blame for an act. necessity plea, ignorance plea, superior-orders rejection responsibility (root) := <<moral element - responsibility / accountability answerability relation binding an act to its agent. steward's account, command responsibility, vicarious liability responsibility (root) := <<moral element - sanction / repair response restoring a breached moral order. apology, restitution, punishment, forgiveness structural (root) := <<moral element - moral compound bounded ensemble scoping a decomposition; the generic compound type. harbor stewardship compact; ward-care compact structural (root) := <<moral element - tradition transmitted morphology of precepts, exemplars, and casuistry. fiduciary care tradition, oath-keeping tradition structural (root) := <<moral element - exemplar concrete model of virtue or vice for imitation or avoidance. conscientious steward, whistleblower, deserter of duty dynamic (root) := <<moral element - consequence foreseeable effect entering the evaluation of an act. harm averted, trust broken, precedent set dynamic (root) := <<moral element - transformation of character habituation-to-corruption or reform trajectory over time. habituation into fidelity; corruption by small concealments dynamic (root) := <<moral element - state complete relevant-variable snapshot of a moral posture at a moment. indebted, compromised, exonerated, entrusted how to decompose any moral instance? a decomposition of a moral instance expands its tree from the root — the conduct under assessment — adding the agents, acts, goods, principles, duties, judgments, and responsibilities that bind, move, verdict, and answer for it. begin with the imputability test: does the agent have capacity, knowledge, and freedom, and what stakes ride on the act? then assign its tradition by governing precepts and exemplars, never by location or actors. then grow the tree. see the worked case in qa below (### (case study) what is the recursively decomposed instance tree of a steward's disclosure?). read the case table as the worked in-path-typed tree: the empty table here is filled the same way, typing each row from its grouping segments and the declared root binding. moral element type tree path: the expansion path typing one instance row — (root) := <<moral element bound to the row's table type, continued by exactly one licensed expansion: a spine-ordered suffix, a tradition attachment, or a composite nesting. in other words, a tree path is what the single table generates. it is a type-level path ( - ), never to be confused with the instance tree path (first column), which strings instances with → . constructing the path: (1) type the instance — find its row in the table above; (2) bind — write (root) := <<moral element as that type; (3) extend — continue with exactly one licensed expansion from the bound position (spine-ordered suffix, tradition attachment under the bound root, or composite nesting); (4) check — single types and spine-ordered chains always license; anything else must match a composite nesting. the tree is governed by the following rules: root: the root is the moral instance being decomposed. structure: intermediate nodes provide the structure needed to organize the decomposition - they can be moral instances - or moral types. moral types cannot be the final nodes in the tree - may be used as grouping nodes, but they are not themselves instances. leaves: every leaf must resolve to a moral instance. typing: every instance is typed — by its nearest enclosing grouping segment, with the decomposition root's type declared once. recursion: any instance in the tree may itself be decomposed recursively. well-formedness: an instance decomposition is well-formed when every instance row's type path is a path the table generates: bind (root) := <<moral element to the root instance's type and continue down-branch in order; branch order is never skipped. any row may serve as a decomposition root for recursive decomposition. no repetition: the root's own type must not be unnecessarily repeated as an intermediate grouping node. exception: a same-type segment is allowed when it scopes a genuine instance family that would otherwise hang untyped (e.g. a duty / obligation grouping scoping the disclosure-duty family inside a stewardship decomposition, whose counterpart is (root) := <<moral element - ... - duty / obligation ); a same-type segment with only generic description and no scoping function stays forbidden. well-form instance tree path rule: ensure the decomposition provides a rich set of intermediate (internals) nodes - both - type and instances, aiding understanding. the set of intermediate instance nodes representing relationships such as binding, grounding, verdicting, answering, repairing, or other useful structural and dynamic relationships. style rules for intermediate nodes instances: style intermediate nodes that represent actual moral instances as plain text (no adornment). naming: name every instance node in title case — capitalize every whitespace- or hyphen-separated word ( harbor compact - harbor compact , stage-entry criterion - stage-entry criterion ); preserve established all-caps acronyms ( api , eu ). type segments keep their table casing. the rule governs node names in instance tree paths only; descriptions stay sentence-case prose. composite instance naming : a composite instance — a nested ensemble (a moral compound , community of responsibility , or sub-domain set), not an ordinary agent, act, or judgment — takes a name ending in set once it sits at a depth greater than 2. depth counts every segment of the instance tree path, backticked type groupings included, the root type grouping being depth 1. at depth 2 or less the suffix is permitted but never required: moral compound - harbor stewardship compact set (depth 2) keeps it, moral compound - ward-care compact set (depth 3) requires it. types: style bare moral element types used as grouping nodes as code . distinction: never style an instance and a type in the same way; the distinction must be immediately visible. grouping types: a type used only to group instances is not itself an instance and must not terminate a branch. the path link - is →. moral element type tree path : in the definition table this column is a template carrying the <<moral element root slot; once the root instance's type is bound ( (root) := … ), the instantiated path contains only concrete moral element types — no expansion patterns or placeholders. instance tree path description moral category moral element type tree path --- --- --- --- how to decompose an instance that belongs to multiple element types? by default, a multi-root forest : one root per candidate type, each root growing its own well-formed tree. no instance row ever carries two types — typing reads from grouping segments and the declared root binding. ambiguity is resolved by multiplication of trees, not by compromise typing. a moral element can belong to many types: a stewardship compact is a moral compound readable as a community of responsibility ; a disclosure is a moral act readable as a duty / obligation discharged; a code is a precept / code readable as a tradition fragment. each reading gets its own root and its own tree: the compact-as-compound tree decomposes agents, acts, and judgments (ensemble members), while the compact-as-community tree decomposes offices, mandates, and mutual answerability (membership content). well-formedness per tree is unchanged — every path must be a path the single table generates; leaves are instances, intermediate nodes give structure. when the root typing is ambiguous, ask the user for disambiguation instead of guessing. if no answer comes, build the default root : a primary type chosen from the table above (the "how can we characterize the moral aspect of human experience?" table), recorded as the note's primary belonging in the "what moral element type does this moral instance belong to?" formulation answer, with secondary readings kept as readable as … prose. the default root is therefore always explicit in the note itself. terminology the terms used across this note — agent, act, good, value, principle, duty, right, judgment, responsibility, sanction, virtue, and the moral family — are defined in the glossarium. qa where do promises and stewardships decompose? promises decompose as moral act s binding promisor to promisee under a duty / obligation grounded in a principle / maxim (fidelity), verdict by moral judgment and held by responsibility / accountability . stewardships decompose as moral compound s: moral agent s with conscience , moral act s of disclosure and care, value / good s at stake, and sanction / repair where trust breaks. neither is single-condition — grow one tree per reading when imputability or typing is contested. what belongs to the social, technical, or epistemic instead? the coordination of roles and institutions belongs to the social decomposition even when morally loaded: decompose the institution socially, the obligation morally, and cross-link. the engineering of means belongs to the technical decomposition even when morally urgent: decompose the device technically, the choice to deploy it morally, and cross-link. the warranting of belief belongs to the epistemic decomposition even when beliefs excuse or condemn: decompose the artifact epistemically, the judgment morally, and cross-link. edit the node where its grammar lives; view it wherever its role applies. what is the most abstract formulation that answerability can take? - claim → deliberation → responsible act. - trust placed → choice owned → account rendered. why is the category moral compound required? a moral compound is required to represent coherent moral ensembles whose members belong to different moral element types but are related through a common charge, trust, or answerability problem. without this category, the taxonomy can describe the individual elements of such an ensemble, but it lacks a type for representing the ensemble itself as a moral entity of organization . take as example: a harbor stewardship compact. it comprises stewards, wards, disclosures, care rounds, safety duties, rights of the ward, deliberations, judgments, and repairs. these elements have different moral element types, but are related through the common scope of holding a harbor community's good in trust. the moral compound category provides a type for representing this coherent ensemble as a whole. why shouldn't moral knowledge be a moral element type? moral knowledge should not be a moral-element type because knowledge is already represented by the taxonomy as a distinct ontological category (principles known, precedents studied, and the epistemic scaffolding that warrants them); making it a moral element would conflate the knowledge about a moral reality with the moral reality itself. what belongs here are the verdicts knowledge leaves behind: principles invoked, duties discharged, judgments rendered, repairs performed. why do we need imputability and traditions? imputability (capacity, knowledge, freedom, stakes) and traditions fill the ontological gap between conduct itself and the decomposition that renders it assessable . imputability states under which standing an act counts as the agent's own — intact or defeated — so the same name under two standings decomposes as two readings. traditions state by which transmitted morphology of precepts and exemplars it is scoped — fiduciary care, oath-keeping, civic stewardship — so inquiry stays scoped without owning nodes. together they provide the standing-plus-morphology structure against which moral elements are typed, deliberated, judged, and answered for. notes.text: philosophia naturalis et operis reality is the total set of phenomena, entities, and processes that exist or occur, independently of an observer's perception or conceptualization, and which can, in principle, interact, change, or produce effects. philosophia naturalis is the scaffolding used to delimit, and render intelligible, observer-independent nature: segmenting the flux, characterizing what the segments contain, and validating the resulting descriptions against what actually exists. this note is the ground of the other three guides. philosophia artium epistemicarum et operis systematizes the scaffolding of inquiry, the social and technical philosophiae the decomposition of their domains — but all of them operate on what this note delimits: reality as the constraint space that resists, confirms, and outruns every representation. for the definitions it presupposes (reality, segment types, levels of organization, the ontology/epistemology dual), see the epistemicarum guide rather than restated here. field observation is a training ground for rigorous natural description because it enforces segment-bound, level-aware, limitation-checked affirmations about what actually exists. the value lies in transferring this ontic discipline — rather than its specific catalogs — into more complex domains like social systems. index formulation what is the nature of natural practice ? natural practice: (reality; observation, inference) → segmented description & validation. a natural activity is any operation performed by an observer to cut, characterize, and validate a segment of observer-independent reality at the appropriate level of organization. what is the natural attitude? segment a piece of reality, characterize its entities, processes, and phenomena at the appropriate level of organization, and validate every affirmation against observation and inference. never mistake the template (segment, system, variable) for the territory: templates are epistemic constructs for parsing, not ontic residents. what is at stake in describing nature? compression plus control: minimize description length while maximizing the ability to explain, predict, and intervene. worth describing are the recurring patterns that buy such compression — and the fundamental limitations (see the checklist below) that bound what any description can achieve. which limitations bound every natural description? apply as a checklist to each decomposed instance: complexity, nonlinearity, uncertainty, chaos, emergence, scale, data availability, computational complexity, irreducibility, partial observability, non-repeatability, measurement disturbance, many-body coupling. each is an ontic property of the segment, not a failure of method — record which ones the instance exhibits. what is the reality we seek to describe? observer-independent reality as delimited above: entities and processes with causal effects, dynamic and interconnected, accessible imperfectly through observation and inference. reality is decomposed for description in the natural order tree below. at which level of organization do we describe? the hierarchical stratification of structural and functional components, from microscopic interactions to emergent macroscopic behaviors — crucial when describing systems with multiscale dynamics, memory, or adaptive laws. - micro-level: individual elements and their local interactions. - meso-level: subsystems, modules, clusters of interactions. - macro-level: emergent patterns, global behavior, systemic properties. what is the ontology of the target? what is nature like as describable? ontology constrains what can be affirmed; its constructs for parsing (segments, entities, processes, phenomena) live in the natural order tree below, and the full ontic template in the ontic order branch of the epistemicarum guide. how can we characterize the natural aspect of reality? a taxonomy that renders the observer-independent furniture of the world intelligible: systems and their constituents, substances, living organization, processes and phenomena, quantities and constraints — across the physical, chemical, biological, and earth domains. the labour of natural description goes hand in hand with a layout of reality — that is its segment template: every descriptive move presupposes a cut over the event stream, and every ontic distinction earns its keep through explanatory, predictive, or interventive use. note: natural element type is recursive. the type of order of every natural element is the natural order ; the single table below holds its branch, (root) := <<natural element (systems, constituents, living organization, manifestations, quantities, constraints). each branch root carries its path and child rows extend it; child descriptions state the role-in-parent, canonical definitions live on root rows. scaffold rows are those supporting, structuring, or bounding description — systems delimiting segments, limitation factors, constraints; the rest are nature's furniture and its manifestations. note on levels: every natural element carries its level of organization (micro: elements and local interactions; meso: subsystems and modules; macro: emergent patterns and systemic behavior). the same name at two levels denotes two nodes, decomposed separately and linked. spines (adapted to nature): composition-spine natural object - building block - substance / matter (entered via a system-kind root: any of natural system, ecosystem, complex system may substitute); manifestation-spine natural process - phenomenon - state - trajectory . living types attach under the bound root element or stand as roots for biotic instances. an instance table may land at any depth of a spine; intermediate levels are structuring types, never skipped. each type with its category, role description, and instances. natural category natural element type tree path description (role) instance(s) --- --- --- --- meta (root) := <<natural element placeholder binding to any row's type: per decomposition it takes the root instance's type, and the path continues down that type's branch in order. := binds the root slot to the instance's type; - steps down containment below. e.g. bound to natural system for a watershed; to organism for a fox system (root) := <<natural element - natural system bounded set of interacting components with relations, inputs/outputs, feedback. solar system; cardiovascular system; watershed system (root) := <<natural element - ecosystem system emphasizing interdependence within an environment; semi-permeable boundaries. biome; coral reef; gut microbiome system (root) := <<natural element - complex system system whose collective behavior resists component-level reduction. climate; ant colony; immune network constituent (root) := <<natural element - natural system - natural object fully specified material particular. a basalt cliff; a redwood; a lithium cell constituent (root) := <<natural element - natural system - natural object - building block - substance / matter stuff-kind individuated by composition and phase behavior. alloy; cellulose; plasma constituent (root) := <<natural element - natural system - natural object - building block compositional unit recurring across systems. atom; amino acid; nucleotide living (root) := <<natural element - organism self-maintaining, reproducing organization (autopoietic). bacterium; fern; fox living (root) := <<natural element - living process temporally extended biological transformation. photosynthesis; clotting; pathogenesis living (root) := <<natural element - adaptation heritable fit between lineage and environment. antifreeze proteins; beak morphology manifestation (root) := <<natural element - natural process causally continuous event sequence. combustion; corrosion; catalysis manifestation (root) := <<natural element - natural process - phenomenon unified explanatory object over events/processes. black-body radiation; action potential; aurora manifestation (root) := <<natural element - natural process - phenomenon - state snapshot configuration at a resolution. charge distribution; allele frequencies manifestation (root) := <<natural element - natural process - phenomenon - state - trajectory ordered state sequence. succession; decay chain; epidemic curve quantity (root) := <<natural element - property measurable attribute. mass; ph; albedo quantity (root) := <<natural element - interaction-derived quantity joint-state quantifier over independent variables. momentum; heat; gravitational force constraint (root) := <<natural element - natural constraint bound imposed by law, material, or scale. light-speed limit; tensile strength; carrying capacity constraint (root) := <<natural element - limitation factor description-bounding property from the checklist above. chaos (weather); irreducibility (turbulence) how to decompose any natural instance? a decomposition of a natural instance expands its tree from the root — the piece of reality under study — adding the systems, constituents, living organization, processes, phenomena, quantities, and constraints that compose, move, and bound it. begin by cutting the segment (what is included/excluded, at which level of organization?), then populate it, then run the limitation checklist, then validate each affirmation against observation. the tree is governed by the following rules: root: the root is the natural instance being decomposed. structure: intermediate nodes organize the decomposition — instances or types. bare types group but never terminate a branch; every leaf resolves to a natural instance. leaves: every leaf must resolve to a natural instance. typing: each concrete instance carries exactly one type path generated by the single table; hybrids (bio-social, techno-natural) grow one tree per reading (multi-root forest). recursion: any instance in the tree may itself be decomposed recursively. well-formedness: an instance decomposition is well-formed when every instance row's type path is a path the table generates: bind (root) := <<natural element to the root instance's type and continue down-branch in order; branch order is never skipped. any row may serve as a decomposition root for recursive decomposition. no repetition: the root's own type is not repeated as a grouping node without scoping function. well-expansion rule: supply rich intermediates — composition, coupling, regulation, and scale relations. style rules for intermediate nodes instances: style actual natural instances as bold . types: style bare grouping types as code . distinction: never style an instance and a type alike. instance tree path description natural category natural element type tree path --- --- --- --- terminology the terms used across this note — system, object, substance, organism, process, phenomenon, state, trajectory, property, constraint, and the natural family — are defined in the glossarium. qa where does the epistemic scaffolding stop and the ontic description start? at the cut: everything on the template side (segment boundaries, variables, scales, representation forms) is scaffolding and belongs to the epistemic decomposition; everything affirmed about the segment's furniture belongs here. when in doubt, ask which side would change if the instruments changed — what survives is ontic. how do technique-laden natural instances decompose? the instrument technically ( guideline/ambiguity resolution.md ), the formation naturally: decompose the device under the technical grammar, the measured reality under this one, and cross-link at the observation interface. which note schema used - in order to document a natural element? (natural element) (intro) formulation what natural element type does this natural instance belong to? what is this natural instance? what is the recursive instance decomposition of this natural instance? references - ... references - notion export modelo/philosophia naturalis (ancestor draft; its ontology/epistemology core already absorbed in the epistemicarum guide) and modelo/nature/conceptual model natural system (138-entity catalog with system/phenomena/biology/physics/chemistry/matter tags; limitation factor table) - philosophia artium epistemicarum et operis (presupposed definitions: reality, segments, levels, duals, dcesa) - philosophia artium technicarum et operis - philosophia socialium et operis

notes.text: philosophia socialium et operis philosophia socialium is the scaffolding used to parse, and render intelligible, association — the patterned interactions through which agents coordinate, constrain, and constitute one another. reality is the total set of phenomena, entities, and processes that exist or occur, independently of an observer's perception or conceptualization, and which can, in principle, interact, change, or produce effects. this note systematizes a philosophy of the social arts that can serve as a conceptual foundation for organizing the ideas used to explain collective life across diverse domains. it is the complement of philosophia artium technicarum et operis (which systematizes intervention) and philosophia artium epistemicarum et operis (which systematizes intelligibility): where those notes ask how reality is transformed and known, this one asks how agents hang together while doing both. formulation what is the nature of social practice ? social practice: (reality; agents, bonds, institutions) → coordinated order & shared meaning. a social activity is any operation performed by agents to associate, coordinate, constrain, or constitute one another toward stabilized collective life. what is the reality we seek to coordinate within? observer-independent reality as the substrate of association: agents, bonds, lifeworld meanings, and institutional, cultural, and material structures that constrain and respond to social action. reality is decomposed for inquiry in the decomposition-tree structure below. at which level of organization do we associate? the hierarchical stratification of structural and functional components, from dyadic encounters to emergent collective orders — crucial when modeling association with nested membership and multi-scale dynamics. - micro-level: individual encounters and their local interactions. - meso-level: groups, organizations, and their coupled interactions. - macro-level: emergent orders, collective trajectories, systemic properties. what is the ontology of the target? what is social reality like as associable? which units, bonds, and coordinators make it up? ontology answers by constraining what can be coordinated; its constructs for parsing (units, relations, roles, norms, coordinators, structures) live in the decomposition-tree structure below, read always against layers and facets. what is the nature of the social ? the social is the interactional dimension of reality: patterns, structures, and norms emerging from the interactions of agents within specific institutional and cultural contexts — rendered tractable through the frame s = <r,a,e,i : reality, the cognitive agentic domain, the environment (including other agents), and interactional dynamics. what is the role of association in human experience? association enables agents to do together what none can do alone and to be, for one another, the environment that constrains and enables action: every agent's e (environment) is substantially composed of other agents' φ (executions). coordination is therefore never a mere aggregation of acts; it is the recursive coupling of decision architectures. what is a social element ? it is a concept that denotes an element participating in the association-oriented and coordination-oriented dimension of collective life experienced by humans or other purposeful agents. note: this is a deliberately loose definition of the reality denoted by the concept. foundation - reality - the ontological substrate comprising the agents, bonds, lifeworld meanings, and institutional, cultural, and material structures that constrain and respond to social action. person, household, firm, river basin, spectrum commons, fiat currency. what grounds social phenomenology ? social practice is grounded in the lived experience of togetherness: intentionality directed at others, mutual recognition, and the lifeworld — the pre-given horizon of shared meanings, typifications, and habitual certainties within which every encounter already finds itself. interaction units (individuals, groups, organizations, polities, networked collectives) and agencies (structured capacities for intention, selection, execution, and feedback) are crystallizations of this phenomenological ground, not its foundation: they name how the self–other pairing stabilizes into recognizable actors, never what makes the pairing possible. what is the structure of a social element's decomposition tree? how can we characterize the social dimension of human experience? a taxonomy (conceptual structure) that renders the social reality intelligible. a social element is a conceptual innovation that denotes a constituent of social reality, analytically identifiable as an instance of a social element type and capable of being recursively decomposed into other social elements through explicitly typed relationships. what is the fundamental structure of a social element's decomposition tree ? social element (parent) (→ <relationship type ) <social element (son) which are some ideas to guide the decomposotion of a social element ? a reference table defining the permitted link forms that govern and standardize the recursive decomposition of a social element into its constituent and related social elements. note: if a social element appears as a parent in a decomposition tree, only the child elements explicitly permitted by this reference table may be included, unless the child elements are defined by a template specified using <<... . note:
