notes.title: Paul Romer
notes.text: paul romer paul romer is known for his significant contributions to economic growth theory and innovation. some of his primary papers include: 1. "endogenous technological change" (1990) : in this seminal paper published in the journal of political economy, romer introduced the concept of endogenous growth theory. he argued that technological progress is not exogenous but rather determined by economic factors such as investment in research and development, human capital accumulation, and knowledge spillovers. this paper laid the foundation for understanding how policies and institutions influence long-term economic growth. 2. "increasing returns and long-run growth" (1986) : this paper, also published in the journal of political economy, explores the role of increasing returns to scale in driving sustained economic growth. romer demonstrates how positive feedback loops can lead to autonomous growth dynamics, challenging the traditional assumption of diminishing returns in economic models. 3. "growth based on increasing returns due to specialization" (1987) : in this paper, romer further develops the concept of increasing returns to scale by focusing on the role of specialization and knowledge accumulation. he highlights how economies can benefit from specialization and trade, leading to higher productivity and growth. 4. "the origins of endogenous growth" (1994) : this paper, co-authored with diego puga, provides an overview of endogenous growth theory's historical and theoretical foundations. romer and puga discuss key contributions to the field and highlight the implications of endogenous growth for understanding the dynamics of technological change and economic development. 5. "economic growth" (2007) : romer's work on economic growth is also encapsulated in his textbook "economic growth," which provides a comprehensive overview of theories, empirical evidence, and policy implications related to economic growth. the book synthesizes romer's research and other economists' contributions, making it a valuable resource for students and researchers in the field. these papers and contributions have profoundly impacted the study of economic growth and development, influencing academic research and policy debates. romer's insights have helped shape our understanding of the drivers of long-term prosperity and the role of innovation in fostering economic progress.

notes.title: Philip Kotler
notes.text: philip kotler philip kotler, often referred to as the "father of modern marketing," is an influential figure in the field of marketing, having authored numerous seminal books and articles throughout his career. some of his main works include: 1. "marketing management" : considered his magnum opus, this book is one of the world's most widely used graduate-level textbooks in marketing. it covers a wide range of marketing principles, theories, and practices. 2. "principles of marketing" : co-authored with gary armstrong, this book is another widely used text that lays out fundamental marketing concepts and strategies for undergraduate students. 3. "kotler on marketing" : this book summarizes kotler's insights on approaching marketing as an integrated set of tools and processes. it offers a concise overview of his marketing philosophy. 4. "marketing 4.0: moving from traditional to digital" : co-authored with hermawan kartajaya and iwan setiawan, this work explores the shift from traditional to digital marketing, emphasizing the importance of technology and online platforms in modern marketing strategies. 5. "marketing insights from a to z: 80 concepts every manager needs to know" : this book provides a comprehensive overview of essential marketing concepts in a concise and accessible format, making it useful for managers and professionals. 6. "marketing 3.0: from products to customers to the human spirit" : also co-authored with hermawan kartajaya and iwan setiawan, this book discusses how marketing has evolved to focus on values and social responsibility, going beyond traditional product-centric approaches. 7. "strategic marketing for nonprofit organizations" : this work applies marketing concepts and strategies to nonprofit organizations, addressing their unique challenges and opportunities. 8. "social marketing: improving the quality of life" : co-authored with ned roberto and nancy lee, this book explores how marketing principles can promote social change and improve public health, safety, and the environment. 9. "the marketing of nations: a strategic approach to building national wealth" : in this book, kotler applies marketing principles to countries and analyzes how nations can improve their competitiveness in the global market. 10. "chaotics: the business of managing and marketing in the age of turbulence" : co-authored with john a. caslione, this book addresses strategies for businesses to navigate and thrive in turbulent economic times. philip kotler's works have profoundly impacted the marketing field, offering foundational theories, practical strategies, and forward-thinking insights into the evolving landscape of marketing and business strategy. references - philip kotler

notes.title: Pieter de la Court
notes.text: pieter de la court pieter de la court was a dutch economist and political theorist in the 17th century. he was known for his contributions to early economic thought and his advocacy for free trade and republican government. here is a table summarizing some of his main ideas: idea description --- --- free trade de la court was a strong proponent of free trade, arguing that allowing the free flow of goods and services leads to greater prosperity and economic growth. against monopolies he criticized monopolies and mercantilist policies, believing they stifled competition and innovation and were detrimental to economic progress. economic liberty de la court emphasized the importance of economic liberty, advocating for minimal government intervention in economic affairs to allow individuals to pursue their interests and maximize wealth. republicanism he advocated for republican forms of government, arguing that they were more conducive to freedom and economic prosperity than monarchies. separation of powers de la court believed in the separation of powers within government to prevent any branch from becoming too powerful and protect individual liberties. meritocracy he supported the idea of meritocracy, where individuals should rise to positions of power and influence based on their abilities and achievements rather than birthright or social status. population and prosperity de la court argued that a large, dynamic population was crucial for a country's prosperity, and he promoted policies that would encourage population growth and economic activity. role of cities he viewed cities as vital centers of trade, industry, and innovation, essential for a nation's economic development and cultural life. education and knowledge de la court believed in the importance of education and the dissemination of knowledge as foundations for economic and social progress. peace and stability he argued that peace and political stability were necessary conditions for economic growth, as they created an environment where trade and industry could flourish. critique of nobility de la court was critical of the nobility and aristocratic privileges, viewing them as impediments to economic and social progress. these ideas reflect pieter de la court's forward-thinking approach to economics and governance, emphasizing free markets, individual liberty, and republican principles as pathways to prosperity and stability. references - pieter de la court

notes.title: Richard Cantillon
notes.text: richard cantillon richard cantillon, an influential 18th-century economist, is known for his seminal work, "essai sur la nature du commerce en général" (essay on the nature of commerce in general). land is the source or matter from which all wealth is drawn; man's labor provides the form for its production, and wealth in itself is nothing but the food, conveniences, and pleasures of life. (cantillon 1755, p. 21. emphasis added) his contributions laid foundational concepts in economics. here is a table summarizing the main ideas from his work: main idea description --- --- entrepreneurial role cantillon emphasized the role of entrepreneurs as risk-bearers who organize production and drive economic activity. cantillon effect he introduced the concept that changes in the money supply affect different groups differently, impacting prices and income distribution. market clearing he discussed the idea of market equilibrium, where prices adjust to balance supply and demand. land rent theory cantillon theorized that land rent is a residual income after deducting production costs, influencing land use and distribution. circulation of money he explored how money circulates through the economy, affecting prices and economic activity. value and price formation cantillon analyzed how the value of goods and services is determined by market forces and how prices adjust accordingly. role of population he noted that population growth impacts economic development, influencing demand, labor supply, and land use. distribution of wealth cantillon examined how wealth is distributed among different social classes and its impact on economic stability. economic uncertainty he highlighted the importance of uncertainty and its influence on economic decisions and entrepreneurship. government and market while not extensively, he touched upon the role of government intervention and its effects on market efficiency. these ideas form the core of cantillon's contributions to economic theory and have influenced subsequent economic thought. references - richard cantillon

headings.text: **Integration with Law, Politics, and the Economy**

notes.text: roberto mangabeira unger roberto mangabeira unger is a brazilian philosopher, legal theorist, and politician whose social theory is one of the most ambitious and original in contemporary thought. his work spans law, politics, economics, and philosophy, and it resists conventional ideological categorization. unger’s core contribution is the idea that social reality is plastic, mutable, and subject to radical innovation —a view he calls "formative context" theory and "radical institutionalism." ideas main idea/concept description --- --- empowered democracy advocates for deepening democracy by increasing citizen participation and decentralizing power. plasticity of social institutions emphasizes that social structures and institutions are malleable and can be reshaped by human action. radical reformism proposes comprehensive and transformative reforms to address systemic social and economic issues. imagination and innovation stresses the importance of creativity and innovation in driving social and economic progress. critique of neoliberalism criticizes neoliberal policies for exacerbating inequalities and limiting democratic control. alternative globalization advocates for a form of globalization that prioritizes social justice, environmental sustainability, and equitable development. human empowerment focuses on empowering individuals through education, technology, and economic opportunities. social solidarity emphasizes the need for social cohesion and collective action to address common challenges. social theory formative contexts unger argues that every society is shaped by formative contexts —deeply embedded institutional and imaginative frameworks that define the limits of social, economic, and political life. unlike structuralist or marxist thinkers, unger believes these contexts are not fixed but radically revisable . human societies are not constrained by immutable laws but are open to deep innovation . these include: - legal and institutional structures (e.g., property, contract, government) - social hierarchies and norms - prevailing ideologies and narratives plasticity of the social “there is no natural or necessary form of social life.” this means that human institutions and practices are inherently malleable , and we can rebuild society in alternative ways through imaginative thought and political action. false necessity and institutional alternatives in his seminal book false necessity: anti-necessitarian social theory in the service of radical democracy (1987), unger argues that: - many social structures are presented as necessary or inevitable (e.g., capitalism, nation-states, legal frameworks) - these necessities are "false" , sustained by ideology and inertia rather than logic or nature - we must explore alternative institutional forms —especially those that deepen democratic participation , flatten hierarchies , and promote self-realization empowered democracy unger calls for an "empowered democracy," which: - goes beyond liberal democracy - involves radical experimentation with new forms of political, economic, and social organization - requires institutional innovations like: - rotating leadership - decentralized decision-making - flexible property regimes - educational systems fostering creative and critical capabilities non-ideal theory with a utopian aim unlike most analytic political philosophers who work within "ideal theory" (e.g., rawls), unger: - works in a "non-ideal" but aspirational mode - tries to imagine and design real alternatives , not just describe justice in theory - believes political imagination is a central intellectual tool —we must design new futures, not just critique the present integration with law, politics, and the economy unger was a key figure in the critical legal studies movement , and much of his early work challenges the neutrality and objectivity of legal reasoning. he integrates his social theory with: - law : law is both a tool of reproduction and a site of creative disruption. - politics : calls for "high-energy politics" —where citizens are engaged in continuous institutional redesign. - economy : advocates for democratizing the market by introducing cooperative, decentralized, and innovative economic models . notable works in social theory - knowledge and politics (1975) - law in modern society (1976) - false necessity (1987) – vol. 1 of politics: a work in constructive social theory - plasticity into power (1987) - democracy realized (1998) phrases - defiance is not always rewarded, but obedience is invariably punished . - human nature & the plasticity of the self - "we are not stuck being the way we are. the human self is not a thing; it is a project." - "human nature is not fixed but formed in history and capable of being reformed by it." - "to be human is to live incompletely—to exist as a being who must make itself." - "each of us is more than the roles society assigns us." - "no social order has the right to claim the entirety of the human personality." - structure, agency, and social transformation - "structures enable and constrain, but they can also be remade." - "the true radicalism is institutional: to reorganize the arrangements of social life to widen the range of human possibility." - "the point is not to destroy structures, but to loosen their grip and multiply their alternatives." - "we must make institutions that give form to our power to reshape them." - democracy, freedom, and empowerment - notes.title: San Isidoro de Sevilla
notes.text: san isidoro de sevilla san isidoro de sevilla was a distinguished scholar, bishop, and doctor of the church, renowned for his pivotal role in compiling and preserving vast arrays of knowledge during the early middle ages, culminating in his masterwork, the "etymologiae.” isidore of seville, a scholar and theologian of the early middle ages, is best known for his extensive encyclopedic work, "etymologiae" (or "origines"). this work is considered one of the earliest encyclopedias in western civilization and was a crucial reference for medieval scholars. principal works by isidore of seville include: 1. etymologiae (the etymologies) : isidore's most famous and influential work, the "etymologiae" is an encyclopedia that aimed to compile all available knowledge at the time. it covers many subjects, including theology, grammar, geography, medicine, etc. the work is structured around the etymology of words, through which isidore sought to understand and explain the world. 2. de natura rerum (on the nature of things) : before the "etymologiae," isidore wrote "de natura rerum," a book on astronomy and natural history. it was one of the early christian treatments of science and sought to reconcile classical knowledge with christian doctrine. 3. historia de regibus gothorum, vandalorum et suevorum (history of the kings of the goths, vandals, and suevi) : this history of the gothic, vandal, and suevian kings is a valuable resource for understanding the early history of these peoples in iberia. 4. chronica maiora (the great chronicle) : this work is a universal history that begins with creation and runs to isidore's present day. it incorporates much of the content from his "history of the kings of the goths, vandals, and suevi." 5. differentiarum libri (books of differences) : this includes two works, "differentiae verborum," which distinguishes between synonyms, and "differentiae spirituales," which deals with ethical and spiritual concepts. 6. sententiae (sentences) : this theological treatise is divided into three books and deals with the doctrines of the trinity, ecclesiology, and christian ethics. isidore's works were highly influential throughout the middle ages, serving as a cornerstone for medieval scholarship, education, and culture. his efforts to preserve and synthesize knowledge from various sources make him a significant figure in the intellectual history of the west. references - isidoro de sevilla - …

notes.title: Saul Bron
notes.text: saul bron most of technological transfer from to the us to the ussr was personaly supervised by saul bron. born in odessa in 1887, he earned his phd in economics at the university of zurich. after the revolution he became the key figure of soviet economic policy, specifically foreign trade saul bron was the member of the supreme economic council and ceo of many state owned companies. he headed the exportkhleb - a company for the grain export to the west and the bank for foreign trade vneshtorgbank. he supervised most of soviet trade with the capitalist countries in 1927 stalin appointed saul bron as the ceo of amtorg trading corporation. theoretically amtorg was an american corporation. in practice though it was a soviet proxy controlled by politburo. it was a monopoly controlling all the soviet-american trade as the head of amtorg, saul bron would personally look for and choose american partners who would help with the soviet industrialization. one of bron's first findings was a detroit industrial architect albert kahn - here you see them signing a contract in 1929 albert kahn associates secure a mega contract on designing and supervising construction of the stalingrad tractor plant. it was modeled after the international harvester milwaukee plant. kahn prepared architectural and engineering drawings including road & railroad access kahn company fully organised the entire process. they procured american materials, machinery, and equipment, provided american experts. to put it simply, stalingrad tractor plant was lego. details were produced in america and assembled in the ussr under the american supervision in 1941 and 1942 stalingrad tractor plant would be the main producer of famous t-34 tanks which contributed so much into the soviet victory. t-34 is glorified as the example of soviet engineering genius. not wrong. but it was assembled on american-built plants and infrastructure next year they scaled up. in 1930 kahn was commissioned to design and supervise almost all soviet industrial construction under the first & second five year plans: more than 550 plants & facilities all over the ussr, all soviet tank, car & tractor industry, etc for 2 billion usd of course mass involvement of american architects and engineers in soviet industrialisation looked problematic. that's why it was disguised. ussr established an enormous government architecture bureau госпроектстрой as a cover for american experts who lived and worked in the ussr kahn engineers operated all over the ussr building "tractor, car, aircraft power plants, foundries, forges, steelmaking and rolling mills; metallurgical, ball-bearing, aluminum, asbestos plants; machinery and tools manufacturing factories; textile mills, food processing plants” kahn knew he's helping ussr to prepare for a war. in 1931 he told: "there is no question about russia’s preparing herself as fully as possible for such an event, nor is there any doubt that many of the newer plants are planned for the production of war materials when needed" while albert kahn was the main planner of soviet industrialization, hundreds of companies participated. arthur mckee company designed and supervised construction of the largest soviet steel plant in magnitogorsk, modelled after the u.s. steel corporation plant in gary, indiana henry ford participated, too. here you see him negotiating with the amtorg chief saul bron. in 1929 he signed a contract to build a gaz vehicle factory in nizhny novgorod, supply it with equipment, machinery and technologies now you make ask, ok, how did the ussr pay for all of it? technological import from the us should have cost hella lots of money. well, that's why stalin had to milk his people dry. to pay for import, he exported all the food abroad. that's the reason of mass starvation, holodomor the narrative of "autarkic" and "self-sufficient" ussr is total bs. soviet industrialisation fully relied on american assistance, expertise and the technological import. and even with it all, ussr still didn't become self-sufficient. it had so many technological bottlenecks

notes.title: Sigismund Schlomo Freud
notes.text: sigismund schlomo freud the issue is not freud himself—his work may be an example of bad science—but his followers should know better and treat his views not as a religion, but as an explanatory framework that must be tested. research which were freud main research problems? area research questions --- --- unconscious processes - how much of mental life occurs outside awareness? - what mechanisms govern unconscious thought? - how do unconscious processes influence conscious behavior and emotions? - how can unconscious content be revealed and studied? instincts and drives - how do sexual (libidinal) and aggressive drives shape mental life? - how are instinctual desires satisfied, repressed, or redirected? - what is the role of drives in motivating behavior and forming personality? mental functioning dynamics - how do the pleasure principle and reality principle regulate thought and action? - how does the mind manage tension between instinctual desires and external constraints? - what mechanisms underlie repression, resistance, and defense? personality development - how do early childhood experiences shape adult personality? - what is the impact of psychosexual stages (oral, anal, phallic, latency, genital) on behavior? - how do family dynamics and parental relationships influence mental and emotional development? psychopathology - what psychic conflicts produce anxiety, hysteria, or neuroses? - how does repression generate psychological symptoms? - what are the roles of defense mechanisms in protecting the ego? - how do early traumas or unresolved conflicts affect later mental health? dreams and symbolism - how do dreams reveal unconscious desires? - what processes (condensation, displacement, symbolization) transform latent thoughts into manifest content? - can dreams provide insight into unresolved conflicts or repressed material? psychoanalytic methods - how can free association uncover unconscious material? - what is the significance of slips of the tongue, jokes, and parapraxes? - how can clinical observation be systematized into a general theory of the mind? - how can psychoanalytic techniques be validated scientifically? mental energy and motivation - how is psychic energy (libido) distributed and transformed? - what is the relationship between energy, tension, and behavior? - how do mental processes conserve or expend energy in different contexts? interpersonal and social influences - how do social interactions and relationships shape personality? - what is the role of cultural norms in regulating instinctual drives? - how do authority, attachment, and family structure influence mental development? model which models does freud used in his works? target system model description --- --- --- human mind topographical model divides the mind into conscious, preconscious, and unconscious regions, describing how thoughts and memories exist at different levels of awareness. human mind notes.title: Sir Robert Gordon Menzies
notes.text: sir robert gordon menzies sir robert menzies, as prime minister of australia for a significant period from 1939 to 1966, had a notable impact on australia's industrial policy during his tenure. here are some key aspects of his industrial policy : 1. protectionism : menzies' government generally favored protectionist policies to nurture domestic industries and shield them from international competition. this approach was in line with the prevailing economic philosophy of the time, which prioritized domestic manufacturing and industrial self-sufficiency. 2. tariffs and trade : menzies implemented policies that increased tariffs on imported goods, aiming to protect australian industries from foreign competition. this protectionist stance was particularly evident in sectors such as manufacturing, agriculture, and textiles. 3. support for key industries : menzies' government provided various forms of support to key industries deemed vital for the country's economic development. this support included subsidies, grants, and other forms of financial assistance to stimulate growth and innovation in strategic sectors. 4. labor relations : menzies' government maintained a stance that generally favored employers in industrial relations matters. it sought to maintain stability in the labor market and minimize disruptions through policies that often favored the interests of businesses over those of organized labor. 5. infrastructure development : menzies' government invested in infrastructure projects to support industrial development, including transportation networks, energy infrastructure, and telecommunications. these investments aimed to facilitate the efficient movement of goods and services, as well as to provide essential utilities for industrial activities. 6. encouragement of foreign investment : while advocating for protectionist measures, menzies also recognized the importance of foreign investment in stimulating economic growth. his government encouraged foreign companies to invest in australia, particularly in sectors where domestic capital was insufficient to fund large-scale projects. 7. focus on economic growth : overall, menzies' industrial policy was guided by a broader focus on promoting economic growth and development. his government sought to create an environment conducive to business investment, innovation, and job creation, with the goal of enhancing australia's overall prosperity. while menzies' industrial policies reflected the economic priorities and challenges of his time, they have been subject to scrutiny and debate in subsequent years, particularly regarding their long-term impact on australia's industrial landscape and economic competitiveness. references - sir robert gordon menzies

geography, culture, politics. 2018 charter schools and their enemies book analysis of education policy; evaluation of charter school effectiveness. knowledge and decisions sowell’s knowledge and decisions powerfully illustrates how dispersed knowledge shapes economic and political outcomes, but his framework has limits. by privileging local problem-solving, he under-theorizes the hierarchical and systemic nature of many real-world challenges. problems differ not only by scale but by interdependence—ranging from personal choices to infrastructural or societal systems. this localist bias leaves his framework less capable of addressing questions of institutional design, such as subsidies for emerging industries, where structured, rule-based coordination is necessary. in short, sowell explains why central planning fails, but provides little guidance for how societies should design intermediate institutions to handle complex, large-scale problems. pre - analysis knowledge is a structured representation of reality that allows an agent—human, artificial, or otherwise—to make reliable inferences, predictions, or decisions. it encompasses information that has been validated, justified, or otherwise confirmed as dependable within a given context. knowledge is fundamentally about how an observer is able to describe or act in the world. problems and decisions can be categorized by their complexity and by the number of actors involved in working toward their solution. book the book is an extension of hayek’s work “on the use of knowledge in society”. it primarily discusses descriptive knowledge, which enables informed decision-making. knowledge and decisions is a rigorous exploration of how knowledge is dispersed in society and how this affects economic, political, and social decision-making. sowell argues that no single individual or centralized authority can possess all the knowledge needed to make optimal decisions; instead, knowledge is often decentralized, context-specific, and tacit. he examines the mechanisms—markets, organizations, and political institutions—that enable societies to aggregate dispersed knowledge and make effective decisions despite inherent limitations. key themes: 1. dispersed knowledge: knowledge exists in fragments across individuals and cannot be fully centralized. 2. decision-making constraints: institutions and social systems must cope with limited knowledge and imperfect information. 3. trade-offs in coordination: centralized vs. decentralized decision-making, efficiency vs. control. 4. role of incentives: proper incentives and feedback mechanisms are crucial to harness dispersed knowledge. 5. limits of expertise: expertise cannot replace the collective information embedded in society. analysis the framing of knowledge in this book is problematic. knowledge enables us to make decisions and solve problems, but sowell treats decisions or problems almost always from a local perspective - or approximately hierarchical equal. in reality, problems exist on a spectrum—ranging from highly local issues (e.g., what type of coffee to buy) to less local or large-scale challenges (e.g., how to repair a city’s sewage system ). in other words, decisions and problems exist within a hierarchy in terms of the systems - and ecosystems that compose organize living; or by the amount of people that are interested - affected by them. let’s consider how, within the framework proposed by this book, subsidies are treated. for instance, when examining subsidies granted to an emerging industry under a defined set of rules—essentially a management framework—it appears that the book does not provide a clear or specific answer to this type of question or problem. this limitation in sowell’s framework can be further developed under the theme of the limits of self-organization . references - https://www.amazon.com/-/es/thomas-sowell/dp/b017v8g6xs - https://archive.org/details/knowledgedecisio00sowe 0 - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/thomas sowellecibi

notes.title: Vannevar Bush
notes.text: vannevar bush vannevar bush was a seminal american engineer, inventor, and science administrator, known for his profound influence on the direction of scientific research in the united states during and after world war ii. here are some of his main works and contributions: 1. "as we may think" : this seminal essay, published in "the atlantic monthly" in 1945, speculated on the future of information storage and retrieval, proposing a machine called the "memex." the memex was envisioned as a mechanical desk that could store books, records, and communications, and it's notably prescient of modern-day personal computers and the internet. 2. the manhattan project : although not a direct creator, bush was instrumental in the administration and funding of the manhattan project through his role as the head of the office of scientific research and development (osrd). he coordinated the efforts of military, industrial, and scientific communities during wwii. 3. osrd (office of scientific research and development) : bush directed this office, which was responsible for the majority of wartime scientific research efforts, including the development of radar and other critical military technologies. the osrd effectively connected the scientific community with the military needs of the u.s. during the war. 4. the national science foundation (nsf) : following wwii, bush authored a report titled "science, the endless frontier," which led to the creation of the national science foundation. this report laid the groundwork for post-war science policies and emphasized the importance of federal funding for scientific research, advocating for science as a key to improving public health, national security, and economic prosperity. 5. early computers and digital networking concepts : beyond the memex, bush's vision and technical expertise influenced the development of early computing and digital networking concepts. his ideas foresaw many aspects of information society, including the structure of what would become the internet. vannevar bush's work significantly shaped modern scientific research and development policies, and his vision for technology foresaw the information age decades before it came to fruition. references - vannevar bush

notes.text: wilhelm von schröder wilhelm freiherr von schröder (1640–1688) was a saxon cameralist and mercantilist in austrian service — member of the royal society, director of the viennese manufacturhaus on the tabor after becher (1677–1683), and imperial chamber councillor in hungary. his work continues becher's program of manufactures and commerce under an absolutist fiscal state. his fürstliche schatz- und rentkammer (1686, eight editions to 1835) is a classic of the literature: a central treasury relying on public loans and paper money rather than taxation, an attack on the guilds, and the doctrine that the ruler's wealth depends on the wealth and well-being of the subjects. schröder links cameralist state-building to english mercantilism — manufactures protected from foreign competition as the key to national wealth. literary production english titles are the editor's literal glosses; no contemporary english translation is known. do not confuse his works with his father's (salzburg chancellor, d. 1663); see ndb 23. type german title english title date scans ---- ------------ ------------- ---: ----- treatise fürstliche schatz- und rentkammer princely treasury and revenue chamber 1686 1752 bsb 1713 dissertation dissertatio de ministrissimo (dt. vom ober-staats-bedienten , 1673) on the chief minister of state 1663 (dt. 1673) — (included in the 1752 scan above) alchemy nothwendiger unterricht vom goldmachen necessary instruction on gold-making 1684 — (included in the 1752 scan above) supplement disquisitio politica vom absoluten fürstenrecht political inquiry into absolute princely right suppl. — (included in later editions above) references - wilhelm von schröder - ndb 23 / adb 32 (deutsche-biographie.de) - schröder profile (het)

notes.text: william b. bonvillian william b. bonvillian is an influential figure in the fields of science and technology policy, particularly known for his insights on innovation systems and the role of government in fostering technological advancements. here are some of the main ideas and themes found in his work: 1. advanced manufacturing : bonvillian has focused on the importance of advanced manufacturing in the united states, advocating for policies that support the development and adoption of new manufacturing technologies. he argues that revitalizing manufacturing is crucial for economic growth and maintaining competitiveness. 2. innovation system challenges : he examines the challenges within the u.s. innovation system, particularly the gaps between research breakthroughs and their commercialization. bonvillian stresses the need for improved mechanisms to bridge this 'valley of death', ensuring that innovations can move from the lab to the marketplace effectively. 3. role of federal r&d : bonvillian has explored the role of federal research and development (r&d) programs in driving technological innovation. he argues for strategic adjustments in federal r&d to better support areas critical to national interests and economic leadership, such as energy and biotechnology. 4. educational reforms for innovation : he advocates for educational reforms that better align with the needs of an innovation-based economy. this includes enhancing stem (science, technology, engineering, and mathematics) education and integrating skills that promote creativity and innovation in problem-solving. 5. policy for science and technology : bonvillian’s work also delves into specific policy recommendations for supporting science and technology development. he has contributed to discussions on how policies can be structured to support emerging technologies, how to structure government-industry partnerships, and the importance of innovation in addressing societal challenges like healthcare and climate change. william b. bonvillian's contributions are particularly valued for their practical implications, offering guidance on how policies can be crafted and implemented to better support technological innovation and economic growth. references - william b. bonvillian

notes.text: william petty sure, here’s a table summarizing the main theories of william petty, a notable economist and statistician from the 17th century: theory description --- --- political arithmetic petty's approach to economic and social analysis using quantitative data to inform policy decisions. he emphasized the importance of empirical data collection and statistical analysis. labour theory of value the idea that the value of goods is derived from the amount of labor required to produce them. petty believed that labor was the fundamental source of value. full employment petty argued for policies to achieve full employment, believing it was essential for economic stability and growth. he advocated for public works and other measures to ensure that everyone who wanted to work could find a job. land and rent theory petty theorized that the value of land and its rent was based on its productivity and location. he introduced the concept of "economic rent," which is the income derived from the ownership of land and other natural resources. quantity theory of money he suggested that the amount of money in circulation in an economy is directly proportional to the level of prices, which is an early formulation of the quantity theory of money. national income accounting petty was one of the pioneers in estimating national income and wealth, laying the groundwork for modern national income accounting and gdp calculations. population and economic growth he believed that population growth was a crucial factor for economic prosperity and that a larger population could contribute to greater economic output and development. these theories collectively contributed to the development of classical economics and the field of political economy. references - buck, peter. headings.text: Rural reform and the hired-labour debate

notes.text: zhao shukai zhao shukai (赵树凯; b. 1959) is a chinese official of rural policy and governance . from 1982 to 1989 he worked at the rural policy research office of the cpc central committee secretariat; from 1990 at the development research centre of the state council. a veteran drafter of china's rural policy documents and a chronicler of the reform-era policy process. career zhao joined the rural policy research office of the cpc central committee secretariat in 1982 and moved to the development research centre of the state council in 1990, where he held posts including director general of the rural department's organisation research office and director general of the information centre. he held short visiting positions at anu, cuhk, duke, harvard, tübingen, and completed executive programmes at harvard kennedy school and cambridge judge. in 2006 he was the main presenter at a politburo group study session. rural reform and the hired-labour debate in deng xiaoping and hired labour (wechat, 26 aug 2024), zhao reconstructs how china accommodated private employment: rural experiments (e.g. guangdong fishpond contracting), the marx "eight-worker" threshold treated as a capitalist cutoff, divided senior leaders (deng xiaoping, chen yun, wan li, hu qiaomu), and the policy researchers—notably du runsheng—who kept contentious wording out of central documents. restrictive instructions were interpreted flexibly and prohibitions left unenforced; the 1989 ban on party members hiring labour was never formally repealed nor enforced. official document writing in notes on official document writing (2020 talk, published 2025), zhao reflects on four decades drafting for leaders: writing "for public purposes, in someone else's name"; the craft as "dancing in shackles" (innovation within institutional constraint); platform support for researchers; learning from classical memorials and western speeches; and persuading leaders so ideas become their own. references - https://www.eastisread.com/p/zhao-shukai-how-china-allowed-private - https://www.eastisread.com/p/zhao-shukai-ghostwriters-of-reform - https://www.eastisread.com/p/zhao-shukai-where-ezra-vogel-got - https://www.pekingnology.com/p/zhao-shukai-pluralism-powered-chinas - https://www.pekingnology.com/p/chinas-rural-reform-a-history-not

notes.title: Zhuge Liang
notes.text: zhuge liang zhuge liang (181–234 ce), also known as kongming (孔明), was a renowned chinese statesman, military strategist, engineer, and scholar during the three kingdoms period. his ideas span military tactics, governance, ethics, and philosophy. 🧠 zhuge liang's core ideas 1. strategic wisdom (兵法 bīngfǎ) - caution over aggression : zhuge advocated strategic patience , using diplomacy, alliances, and deception over brute force. - "empty fort strategy" : a psychological tactic where weakness is masked as strength to deter enemies—illustrating his belief in using intelligence over force. - flexibility : emphasized adapting plans to changing conditions—a principle resembling sun tzu’s teachings. 2. meritocratic governance - promoted officials based on talent and virtue , not lineage or loyalty. - wrote the "chu shi biao" (出师表) —a memorial to emperor liu shan advising good governance, loyalty to the people, and restraint in the use of power. 3. moral leadership (仁政 rénzhèng) - argued that legitimacy comes from benevolence, ethical rule, and the people’s welfare . - saw the ruler’s job as a moral guide, not just a sovereign. - believed in internal discipline and moral self-cultivation for administrators. 4. administrative efficiency - reformed shu han’s bureaucracy with focus on: - clear legal codes. - fair tax systems. - anti-corruption measures. - emphasized responsibility and accountability , believing in detailed record-keeping and supervision. 5. technological and logistical ingenuity - credited with inventions like the "wooden ox" (木牛流马) —a kind of wheelbarrow for food transport. - master of logistics: ensured sustained supply lines during long campaigns. 6. long-term vision - advocated a gradualist approach to reunifying china, seeing sustainability more important than short-term victories. - repeatedly warned against rash military action without thorough planning. 📜 famous quotes (translated): - “opportunities multiply as they are seized.” - “those who are benevolent are invincible.” - “do not be ashamed of mistakes and thus make them crimes.” 📚 influence zhuge liang is often cited alongside confucius for his moral teachings and alongside sun tzu for his military acumen. his ideas remain relevant in: - leadership and organizational ethics. - military academies (strategy and logistics). - chinese political thought and folklore.

notes.title: Product Development Center

headings.text: What social element type does this social instance belong to?
What is the recursive instance decomposition of this social instance?

notes.text: product development center a product development center is a deliberately structured collective actor that converts a product idea into a realizable product: it holds both halves of product development — realizing the product and developing the technical methods that make and test it — under one management, between a sponsoring firm that states the need and a manufacturing operation that absorbs the outcome. formulation what social element type does this social instance belong to? product development center belongs to the collective / organization social element type — a compound interaction unit carrying its own agencies, roles, and practices. it is not an institution (it is a deliberate actor rather than a stabilized system of rules), not a social field (it is one actor inside a field rather than the field itself), and not an activity (it hosts activities rather than being one). its layer is ontic : the center exists extra-mentally, with an address, a staff, a charter, and a budget. its facet is technical-economic — its dominant causal mechanism is the conversion of development capability into a deliverable offer. read also, secondarily, as an interaction unit in the plain sense: a bounded entity capable of interaction, here nested inside a sponsoring firm and connected to suppliers, universities, and certification bodies. that secondary reading is prose, not a second root; the tree below is typed once. what is this social instance? a product development center is an organization whose mandate is product development — the work of carrying a product from concept to a validated, deliverable offer. product development = product realization + technical method development the two constituents are distinct, jointly necessary, and routinely unbalanced inside a single organization: - product realization fixes what the product is and builds the physical or digital realization that satisfies it — requirement clarification, concept generation, feasibility study, prototype fabrication, design validation, pilot run. its output is a product that exists and meets a stated requirement. - technical method development fixes how the product is made and judged and develops the processes, design rules, test methods, and measurement methods the realization depends on. its output is a method that can be repeated by people who did not write it. a center strong in realization but weak in method development ships products that cannot be produced twice; a center strong in method development but weak in realization holds excellent process knowledge attached to no product. holding both under one management is precisely what distinguishes the center from a research institute (method without a product mandate) and from a manufacturing plant (realization without method development). what is the recursive instance decomposition of this social instance? boundary: one product development center, decomposed by middle depth notes.title: Public Organization

headings.text: What social element type does this social instance belong to?
What is the recursive instance decomposition of this social instance?
Which are the dimensions that make the government agency space?
How do autonomous statutory, incorporated-administrative, executive-agency, Swedish-agency and crown-corporation forms differ?

notes.text: public organization a public organization is an organization wielding delegated public authority under law — the government subtype of organization, spanning ministries, arm's-length agencies, state-owned enterprises, municipalities, and public-private hybrids. formulation what social element type does this social instance belong to? public organization belongs to the collective / organization social element type — a compound interaction unit with identity, membership, and rules, carrying its own agencies, roles, and practices. it is the government subtype of organization: what individuates it is not its internal machinery (shared with every organization) but its constitutive relation to public authority — created or chartered under law, directed toward public purposes, and answerable through political oversight. its layer is ontic : ministries, agencies, and municipal bodies exist extra-mentally, with staff, premises, budgets, and address. its facet is political — its dominant causal mechanism is authoritative rule-execution. legal-instrument readings (statutes, charters) and economic readings (fees, commercial revenue) are prose here, not separate trees. what is this social instance? a public organization fixes who exercises public authority and how : the legal charter, the political principal to whom it answers, the agencies that form intention and select action, the internal governance stabilizing coordination, and the recurrent practices through which it serves, regulates, or trades. canonical instances: ministry, public agency, state-owned enterprise, municipal organization, nonprofit public-private organization. what is the recursive instance decomposition of this social instance? boundary: one generic public organization — direct subtypes plus the governance chain, at shallow depth. the full recursive expansion of the agency forms (statutory, incorporated-administrative, swedish, uk executive) and of the crown corporation lives in the type branch of organization and is not duplicated here. stopping rule: a row is terminal when it names a subtype, an agency, a role, a norm, an obligation, or a practice. identity: instance tree path is the stable identifier of each row; every path is unique. instance tree path description --- --- collective / organization (→ part) public organization organization wielding description --- --- --- legal constitution statutory basis own-act creation with legal personality (autonomous statutory public agency) vs. executive creation (uk executive agency, swedish government agency) direction autonomy from ministerial direction no individual ministerial rule, under collective government decision (swedish); framework-document autonomy (uk); managerial autonomy within minister-set medium-term objectives (japan iaa) control ownership and control wholly public vs. mixed public-private (nonprofit public–private organization) resourcing funding source budget appropriation, fees, or commercial revenue purpose function policy direction (ministry), operation (public agency), or commercial enterprise (state-owned enterprise, crown corporation) how do autonomous statutory, incorporated-administrative, executive-agency, swedish-agency and crown-corporation forms differ? along the five dimensions above: the autonomous statutory public agency draws autonomy from its own statute and legal personality; the (japan) incorporated administrative agency trades incorporation for bounded autonomy inside minister-set objectives; the uk executive agency trades a framework document for operational autonomy without separate legal personality; the swedish government agency is constitutionally insulated from individual ministerial command while remaining under collective government direction; the crown corporation sits at the commercial pole — crown-owned, board-governed, revenue-funded — bordering the private organization reading. references - notes.text: geoscience australia geoscience australia is the australian government's national geoscience agency, seated in canberra: the body that maps the continent, watches it move, positions everything on it, and publishes what it learns. it runs the national earthquake monitoring, the positioning australia precise-positioning capability, the digital earth australia free-and-open satellite-data program, and — since july 2024 — resourcing australia's prosperity, a 35-year, $3.4 billion mapping of the country's resources for the net-zero transition. alongside sits an education centre, open data and publications, and a recently convened first nations advisory group. it is the sibling that is not a university and not a firm: it surveys rather than teaches for degrees, and it publishes precompetitive data rather than extracting for profit — the public ground on which explorers, planners, and emergency managers stand. framed per philosophia socialium et operis. formulation what social element type does this social instance belong to? geoscience australia belongs to the collective / organization social element type — a compound unit with identity, membership, and rules. it is a national survey: a statutory agency, a chief executive and divisions, scientific and technical staff, observatory and positioning networks, data archives, and an australian public as constituent. it is a narrower and more operational unit than the government that warrants it, which is why the branches below carry surveying, monitoring, positioning, publishing, and teaching alongside endowment and mandate. the institution reading — the commonwealth warrant, its standing as the authoritative source of national geoscience, and the open-data norms it polices — is declared as a secondary reading and decomposed below as legitimacy , norm / regulation , and right / obligation . what is this social instance? the commonwealth's geoscience body: scientists, technicians, and administrators in canberra and the field, running seismic stations, positioning networks, satellite-data pipelines, mapping campaigns, and school programs — and publishing the continent's geology, groundwater, hazards, and location information as open data for industry, government, researchers, and the public. layer. ontic — the agency, its staff, its observatories, its archives, and its positioning infrastructure exist extra-mentally. its maps, datasets, and storymaps are noetic instruments; the expectation that a country can know its own ground and navigate it precisely is the shared anticipation it serves. facet. ideational , by dominant mechanism, with an operational face: geoscience australia is reorganized by the production and publication of geoscience, and it is only partly a market-facing actor. its data is a function for others' decisions, not its own product; the authoritative map and the timely warning are the core. boundary. the agency as a body: warrants, divisions, roles, activities, rules, data rights and public duties, relations, resources, run, and present state. the earth science it applies is epistemica; the miners, farmers, and builders who use its data are social and production; the ground itself — shaking, mineralized, water-bearing — is nature. school visits and graduate programs belong here as activity, not as a university's degree power, which this body does not hold. lineage (to verify against the agency's history page at next pass): colonial geological surveys → the bureau of mineral resources → the australian geological survey organisation → geoscience australia in its present statutory form → the satellite-data turn (digital earth australia, 2018) → the 35-year resourcing australia's prosperity mandate from july 2024, with the first nations advisory group convened in 2026. what is the recursive instance decomposition of this social instance? boundary: a middle-depth decomposition of one organization — its warrants, units, roles, activities, rules, obligations, relations, resources, run, present state, expectations, and self-image, each worked to instance leaves. units are decomposed to the level at which they carry their own mandate; individual datasets and school lessons appear only where they evidence a rule. typing reads from the path: the root binds collective / organization ; each branch lands on a flat facet type, except the internal-unit branch, which nests a collective / organization scoping the agency's own programs under the recursion rule for that composite. bare type rows group and never terminate a branch; every leaf is a bold social instance. instance tree path description social category social element type tree path --- --- --- --- collective / organization (→ part) notes.text: fraunhofer society tags: observatorio id: pro-1419 l: 18 status: not started the fraunhofer-gesellschaft model is a unique and successful approach to applied research and technology development. the following vital principles characterize it: 1. applied research focus : fraunhofer-gesellschaft is dedicated to applied research, emphasizing the practical application of scientific knowledge and technological advancements. their research projects are driven by solving real-world challenges the industry and society face. 2. public-private collaboration : fraunhofer collaborates closely with both public and private sectors. they work with government agencies, universities, and private companies to develop technology solutions and innovations. 3. industry relevance : research projects conducted by fraunhofer-gesellschaft are directly relevant to industry needs. they aim to foster innovation, enhance competitiveness, and accelerate technology transfer to the market. 4. interdisciplinary approach : fraunhofer institutes often bring together multidisciplinary teams of experts, including scientists, engineers, and industry specialists. this approach ensures a holistic perspective in addressing complex challenges. 5. regional institutes : fraunhofer operates numerous research institutes across germany, each focusing on specific technology domains. these institutes are integrated into regional innovation ecosystems and work … intermediate role - bridging firms with universities - most of its r&d institutes are located in universities - directors of these institutes mostly have professor titles. - most came from universities, while some were from industry (and later appointed as professors) - undergraduate students start working as research assistants and continue working during their master's degree and ph.d. after graduation, they can work for 3-5 years before leaving for the industry.

notes.text: federal agency for breakthrough innovation (sprind) sprind — the bundesagentur für sprunginnovationen (legally sprind gmbh) — is germany's federal agency for breakthrough innovation: a public, arm's-length funder that discovers research ideas with disruptive potential and develops them toward market, on the model of the us darpa. formulation what social element type does this social instance belong to? sprind belongs to the collective / organization social element type — a compound interaction unit with identity, membership, and rules, carrying its own agencies, roles, and practices. it is a public agency : an operational arm executing mandated functions at arm's length (cf. government organization → type → public agency in the organization note). it is not an institution (it is a deliberate actor rather than the stabilized rules — though it hosts institutions such as its funding governance), and not a research institute (it funds and develops; it does not itself perform laboratory research). its layer is ontic : sprind exists extra-mentally, with staff, premises, budget, subsidiaries, and address in leipzig. its facet is innovation/economic — the dominant causal mechanism is publicly funded breakthrough-innovation coordination. readable secondarily as an institution (the stabilized funding regime it anchors): that reading is prose here, not a second root; the tree below is typed once. what is this social instance? the german federal breakthrough-innovation agency: founded by notarial act in october 2019 after a 2018 government decision and a 2019 founding commission, seated in leipzig, with the federal government (bund) as shareholder and a mandate from the education/research and economy ministries. led by founding director rafael laguna de la vera with a ten-member supervisory board from science, business, ministries, and politics; some fifty staff and roughly €250 million in annual means against a planned €1 billion over ten years. its instruments are start-up funding, investments and convertible loans, research-and-development funding, staged challenges , and short funken demonstration sprints. the sprind freedom act (passed november 2023, in force december 2023) entrusted it with the federal breakthrough-innovation task, freed its financing, and let it found subsidiaries and take equity; a 2025 evaluation judged the agency on mission. worked projects include the gicon height wind tower (via its beventum gmbh subsidiary) and the sovereign tech fund. what is the recursive instance decomposition of this social notes.title: Tecnalia
notes.text: tecnalia tecnalia is one of the largest private applied research and technological development centers in spain and a key player in european innovation. its mission centers on transforming technological research into prosperity and competitiveness for industries and society. note: extensive used of chatgpt; so double check. technology domains tecnalia operates across a broad set of technological domains, often aligned with societal and industrial challenges: - digital transformation: ai, iot, cybersecurity, data analytics. - advanced manufacturing: robotics, additive manufacturing, and automation. - energy transition: renewable energy systems, storage, hydrogen, and smart grids. - sustainable mobility: evs, smart transport systems. - construction & urban habitat: smart buildings, circular economy, digital twins. - health and food: biomedical engineering, personalized medicine, sustainable food systems. industry services tecnalia provides r&d and innovation services to companies, including: - custom technological solutions tailored to client needs. - technology scouting and foresight. - prototyping and pilot plant development. - testing, certification, and regulatory compliance. - digitalization and sustainability consulting. - open innovation and collaborative projects with industry. hr tecnalia’s human resources strategy emphasizes: - talent attraction and retention: with a focus on stem disciplines. - professional development: ongoing training, career progression frameworks, and leadership programs. - diversity and inclusion: initiatives to promote gender equity and multicultural teams. - collaborative culture: promoting multidisciplinary project teams and knowledge sharing. tecnalia vectures tecnalia ventures is the organization's technology transfer and venture building arm. it focuses on: - commercializing research outputs through startups and spin-offs. - supporting deep-tech entrepreneurship, often in sectors like energy, health, and digitalization. - venture creation process that includes validation, incubation, acceleration, and investment. - bridging science and market via business mentoring, ip management, and venture funding networks. internationalization tecnalia maintains a strong global presence through: - participation in eu-funded research programs (e.g., horizon europe). - offices and partnerships abroad in latin america, europe, and asia. - international industrial clients and consortiums. - a strategy focused on cross-border collaboration and technology export. room for improvement yes, tecnalia , like any large r\&d organization, can be improved. below are strategic and structural improvement areas that would enhance its impact, efficiency, and global competitiveness: 🔍 1. sharpen strategic focus current challenge : wide scope of activities can dilute impact and reduce clarity for stakeholders. improvement : define sharper technological "bets" in fewer high-impact areas (e.g., industrial decarbonization, autonomous systems, ai + manufacturing). benefit : stronger brand identity, clearer value proposition, better resource allocation. 🚀 2. accelerate technology-to-market pathways current challenge : like many research institutions, tech transfer can be slow and fragmented. improvement : streamline the pipeline from lab to market. foster tighter industry-research integration (e.g., embedded researchers, industry co-ownership). empower tecnalia ventures with more risk capital and autonomy. benefit : faster commercialization, more successful spin-offs, higher roi from r\&d. 🌍 3. strengthen global positioning current challenge : strong european presence but limited visibility in asia, the us, and africa. improvement : form alliances with top global research institutes and tech hubs. attract foreign industrial clients and talent. position as a global deep-tech incubator , not just a spanish/eu rto. benefit : increased prestige, funding diversification, and strategic influence. 🧠 4. reinforce talent strategy current challenge : high competition for top researchers and technologists. improvement : create elite research tracks with global recruitment. introduce entrepreneurial sabbaticals or intrapreneurship tracks. use equity or revenue-sharing models in spin-offs to retain innovators. benefit : higher talent retention and performance, stronger internal innovation. 📊 5. enhance impact measurement current challenge : outputs often measured by project completion or ip, not real-world impact. improvement : use outcome-based metrics : economic impact on client firms, sustainability kpis, jobs created through spin-offs. publish annual impact reports with sector-specific case studies. benefit : improved accountability, clearer societal contribution, better funding cases. 🕸 6. modernize internal collaboration tools current challenge : silos between research groups or units. improvement : adopt knowledge graphs or internal "talent maps" for cross-pollination. use ai-driven project matching to link researchers with complementary skills. benefit : more innovation from interdisciplinary teams, fewer redundant efforts. history notes.title: Norwegian Institute of Bioeconomy Research (NIBIO)

headings.text: What social element type does this social instance belong to?
What is the recursive instance decomposition of this social instance?

notes.text: norwegian institute of bioeconomy research (nibio) nibio is norway's national research institute for the bioeconomy: it produces the knowledge, the administrative support, and the sectoral competence that the food, forest, and other biobased value chains run on. it was created on 1 july 2015 by merging three institutes — bioforsk, the norwegian forest and landscape institute, and the norwegian institute for agricultural economics research — and inherits working institutions with roots back to 1889. it is the instrument through which norwegian agricultural research became one body rather than five. before the merger, plant genetics, forest, agricultural economics, and applied agricultural research sat in separate institutes with separate mandates and separate relationships to the state. after it, they answer to one board, under one ministry, from one site at ås. the institute defines the bioeconomy it serves in its own words: an economy that exploits biological resources from land and sea, and waste, as inputs for food, energy, and other goods and services. framed per philosophia socialium et operis. the science it produces is decomposed as agricultural science and earth science; the instruments it runs are technique; the farming economy it serves is production. formulation what social element type does this social instance belong to? nibio belongs to the collective / organization social element type — a compound unit with identity, membership, and rules. it is a body: a staff, a board, five divisions, fifteen locations, a mandate, a budget line. what makes it an organization rather than merely an institution is that the organization is the thing that does the work — the divisions are the members, the board is the rule-making body, and the mandate is the warrant they act under. the institution reading is nonetheless real and is declared rather than hidden: nibio is a forvaltningsorgan med særskilt fullmakt og eget styre — an administrative agency with special authorization and its own supervisory board — and the stabilized configuration of roles and rules that makes it answerable to a ministry is exactly the tabular view's institution case, the same case as a central bank. per the multi-root rule that reading takes its own root in its own decomposition; here the statutory configuration is decomposed beneath the organization, as legitimacy , norm / regulation , and right / obligation . no row below carries two types. what is this social instance? a state research institute: researchers, technicians, and advisory staff in five divisions, working on food and plant production, environment, climate, mapping and geodata, land resources, genetic resources, forestry, and the economics of the firms and communities in those sectors — delivering research, administrative support to the ministry, and nationally responsible competence in its fields, for preparedness as much as for policy. layer. ontic — the institute, its staff, its board, its divisions, its sites, its laboratories, and its legal personality exist extra-mentally and would survive any observer. its datasets and mapping products are noetic instruments; the warrant that the food chain's future is knowable in advance is a shared anticipation, and the bioeconomy is the image the institute carries of what it is for. facet. ideational , assigned by dominant causal mechanism rather than by location: nibio is reorganized by the production and circulation of knowledge, and its outputs are warranted by validation rather than by throughput. its laboratories and field stations are instruments it operates, not the mechanism that reorganizes it. boundary. this note covers the organization: its mandate and warrants, its divisions, its roles, its activities, its rules, its obligations, its relations, its resources, its run, and its present shape. it does not decompose the science (epistemica), the instruments (technique), or the farmers and firms in the value chains it serves (social and production). a division is decomposed to the level at which it carries its own mandate; a project is an exemplar only where it evidences a rule. lineage: scattered agricultural experiment stations and forestry research under a 1889 statute → post-war institutes of applied agricultural research, forest research, agricultural economics, and plant breeding, each with its own directorate → the 2014 decision to merge five bodies, announced in june of that year → establishment on 1 july 2015 with bioforsk, skog og landskap, and the agricultural economics institute inside one board → consolidation of five divisions and the build-out of the national data services (kilden, vips, agromet.no) as the institute's institutional form of long-term monitoring. what is the recursive instance decomposition of this social instance? boundary: a middle-depth decomposition of one organization — its warrants, internal units, roles, activities, rules, obligations, relations, resources, run, present state, expectations, and self-image, each worked to instance leaves. internal units are decomposed to the level at which they carry their own mandate; projects, people, and publications appear only where they evidence a rule. typing reads from the path: the root binds collective / organization ; each branch lands on a flat facet type, except the internal-unit branch, which nests a collective / organization scoping the institute's own members under the recursion rule for that composite. bare type rows group and never terminate a branch; every leaf is a bold notes.text: norwegian institute for air research (nilu) nilu is an independent norwegian research foundation founded in 1969 to study air pollution, and now a climate and environmental research institute measuring the atmosphere, the contaminants in it, and the health effects of both. it runs observatories in the arctic, antarctica, and norway, holds the national responsibility for air-pollution research, and is consulted by the world bank, the who, and the wmo. it is not a state agency. nilu is a private non-profit foundation that holds a public basic grant and competes for the rest of its income, and that distinction is the reason it sits here rather than beside nibio as one more state institute. framed per philosophia socialium et operis. formulation what social element type does this social instance belong to? nilu belongs to the collective / organization social element type — a compound unit with identity, membership, and rules. it is a foundation: a registered legal person (organization number 941 705 561), a board, a staff, and research groups. the foundation form is not a detail here — it is what makes the institute's independence a rule the body is organized to protect, rather than a property of being inside a ministry. the board appoints a chief executive; the staff are answerable to the board; the money comes from grants the institute must win. the institution reading — the stabilized configuration of roles and rules around a national responsibility, the air-pollution mandate the state leans on — is real and is declared as a secondary reading under the multi-root rule. it is decomposed below as legitimacy and activity ; no row carries two types. what is this social instance? an independent environmental research foundation: atmospheric scientists, chemists, and technicians running measurement stations and accredited laboratories, and delivering monitoring, modelling, and assessment to the state, to industry, and to international bodies — with a third of its income from sources outside norway and a fifth of its staff born outside it. layer. ontic — the institute, its staff, its laboratories, its observatories, and its legal personality exist extra-mentally. its measurement series are noetic instruments; the expectation that the atmosphere can be held to account across decades is the shared anticipation that organizes the work. facet. ideational , by dominant causal mechanism: nilu reorganizes itself around producing and circulating measurement knowledge, and its services are the delivery form of that knowledge rather than a market-facing business. boundary. the institute as a body: its warrants, groups, roles, activities, rules, obligations, relations, resources, run, and present state. not the atmospheric science itself (epistemica), not the instruments it operates (technique), not the industry that buys its services (social and production). lineage: an institute created in 1969 for air-pollution research, when smog and acid rain made measurement a national necessity → expansion into atmospheric composition, climate change, and health effects as those fields became measurable → polar observatories, with a permanent arctic presence from 1973 and scientific responsibility for the zeppelin station → a service and consultancy business whose revenue now exceeds its grant, and a research position maintained largely on european and international money. what is the recursive instance decomposition of this social instance? boundary: a middle-depth decomposition of one notes.text: norwegian institute for nature research (nina) nina is norway's leading institution for applied ecological research: an independent foundation, established in 1988, that delivers research-based knowledge and solutions for nature management to authorities, business, and the public. it monitors what the country is losing — large carnivores, wild salmon, seabirds, pollinators, insects — and runs the national nature index that records the trend. its work is a long record rather than a series of projects: monitoring programmes that hold a series across decades, breeding stations that keep a population alive in order to study it, and an institute that is, by its own account, most of its income commissioned by the environmental authority. framed per philosophia socialium et operis. formulation what social element type does this social instance belong to? nina belongs to the collective / organization social element type — a compound unit with identity, membership, and rules. it is a research foundation: a private non-profit with its own board of trustees, a managing director, eight area directors forming a central management group, and roughly three hundred staff. the foundation form matters to how the institute works: it is chartered to act for nature and society rather than for a ministry, which is what lets it assess the consequences a client would prefer not to hear. the institution reading — the standing configuration of roles and rules behind national monitoring responsibility — is declared as a secondary reading, decomposed below as legitimacy and activity . what is this social instance? an independent ecological research foundation: natural scientists and social scientists in eight areas, running long-term monitoring of species, habitats, and ecosystem condition, impact assessments, advisory services, and research stations for wild salmonids and arctic fox — delivering most of its work to the environmental authority and publishing the national state of nature. layer. ontic — the foundation, its staff, its stations, and its records exist extra-mentally. its monitoring series are noetic instruments; the expectation
